Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 17, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act.

225S
Soldier Settlement Act
I presume the motion is printed or the second reading would not be moved?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We announced last night that we would take it up.

I am aware of that. I rise only to say that I am not aware of the contents of the bill with reference to the special feature that was under debate, and in so far as that special feature relates to the principle of the bill, I do not wish the fact that we agree to the motion for the second reading to be taken as an acceptance of that feature of the principle.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Revaluation of land sold to settlers.

May I ask the minister whether he is prepared to include those who may technically not be on the land, but who have done a certain amount of improvement work, and have resided on the land for, say, a minimum of five years? Is he prepared to put them on the same basis as those who come in under the empire settlement scheme and take up land?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. I may say that there is a considerable number of changes in the bill, though no changes in the first page of the bill. Probably I had better read the clause proposed with respect to revaluation.

Can we not have a
copy of the changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was hoping to have a reprint of the changes ready. I have not got them at the moment, but they may be here a little later. The proposed new clause (c) of section 68 reads as follows:
The difference or depreciation in value to be determined shall be the diminution, not due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler, in the present market value of the land as compared with the price at which the settler agreed to purchase the said land from the board provided that in any case where the- actual sale price is greater than the maximum amount which under section 16 of this act may be advanced by the board in the purchase of land on behalf of any settler, such maximum amount shall be deemed the sale price for the purposes of this section.
There are several cases where the board was willing to pay, say for example, SI,000, but where the settler himself was so anxious to secure the land that he paid, say, $1,000 more. That $1,000 will not be taken into considera-

tion in any revaluation, but simply the maximum amount paid for the land by the board.
I am afraid the minister did not get my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was coming to that, but first I wanted to review briefly the provisions of this section.
With respect to the man who is now off the land and the man who is paid up on his land, their contracts are closed out, and they will receive no consideration.
Then there is another case, that of the man who purchased for, say, $3,000. He purchased at that price and paid nothing further himself. He has paid off all his indebtedness, we will say, except for the sum of $800. If in the revaluation he was entitled to a reduction of $1,000, there would be coming to him $200, but under the provisions of this section he will be credited only with $800; he will not be credited with anything further than the amount of his indebtedness to the board.
That is the way it was before; it is that way still?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The case I had in
mind was that of a man who has put in four or five years in occupancy and development and who is technically off the land, but has na desire whatsoever to abandon it, and whose contract has not been closed1 out in the sense of his land having been disposed of to someone else. Will he be put on the same basis as t'he new purchaser of the land? I am asking particularly with regard to the man who has put in, say, five years on the land, and has done from, say, one to two thousand dollars' worth of improvements. If he now desires to get the benefit of revaluation and resume possession and continue on the farm, will he be considered under this act, or is the man who comes in under the empire settlement scheme going to get the preference over the returned soldier who has put in five or six years on the farm and actually done work showing that he is a capable farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid section 68 (a) would cut him out, because he has to foe actually residing on the land. I have not made any change in clause (a).

There are some men
who for the purpose of making a little money, and with no desire to abandon their land, have gone away, and technically they may be off the land, but if they now desire to continue under this revaluation, will the government consider their case?

Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I could not go outside the limitations of the act, and section 68 (a) says very plainly:
Application for revaluation can be considered only when made by a settleT residing on and himself fanning the said land.

I understand the minister to mean there the man who has definitely abandoned his land, but I am drawing his attention to the case of the man who did not wish to abandon his land, but found it impossible to stay on it for the time being, and I am asking if a preference is going to be given to the man who is coming out to Canada under the empire settlement scheme. Is the new settler to be given the right to buy at a lower price, but not the returned man who has put in many years on the land, and who now desires to purchase at the reduced valuation?

Perhaps
we can get at it in a different way. Is it not possible that t'he man to whom the hon.
. member for Selkirk refers could go back on the land and1 then make application for revaluation? Would not that meet the case?
That would be satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In that case of course he would come within the provisions of the act as he would be actually residing on the land at the date he made his application.

The minister does not quite understand my point. If a man has been technically off the land for years, having actually determined that unless there was a revaluation it would be hopeless for him to continue, but now under a revaluation he would like to continue, is he not to be given a chance?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is, his contract is not cancelled, it is still in existence. If he moves back to his farm and takes up actual residence, he comes within the provisions of the act.
Would the minister undertake to say that the application of any settler who wants to continue on his land will be considered within two months of the passing of this measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would say most emphatically that if he is on the land at the date he files his application, then he comes within the provisions of the act, and whether it is within two months or up to the date it must terminate, his application will be received.

But the minister will remember that when this matter was first under discussion both the member for Neepawa (Mr. Murphy) and I drew attention to the men whom the board had tried to put off their lands. It is those men who are not now actually physically off the land that I am dealing with. If within two months of the passage of this bill they come back and say they want to continue on their land and come within the class who have been five years or more on the land and have done improvements to the extent of SI,500, will they be allowed to come in under the revaluation scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I think I would go further than that. I propose to amend the act by giving six months from the date of the passage of the act for the final filing of applications, so if the men were actually in residence four months after this measure becomes law they would come within its provisions.
And in the meantime those lands will not be disposed of under the allotment to the Empire Settlement Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have been discussing the matter with the chairman of the Soldier Settlement Board, and he is extremely anxious that urgency be used in clearing this matter up, for the very reason that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Hannesson) has mentioned, that a large number of men are waiting to see what is going to happen in the revaluation before they come to a final decision as to whether they will continue on their land or not. That is why we first thought of giving a year from the passage of the act for the filing of claims, but I have suggested that we reduce that time to six months in order that we might facilitate the operation of the act.
In the meantime the minister will not-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg your pardon. No action would be taken to dispossess any man until he had had an opportunity to make a final decision.

I understand that under the empire settlement agreement a certain number of units have been promised, and that some work has already been done on them. Will the minister give the House an assurance that so far as the soldier settlement lands are concerned none of the units that pertain to any of those men who have not been absent more than a year will be
Soldier Settlement Act

allotted under the empire settlement scheme, so as to afford those boys an opportunity to come back?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unless the land was going to be left idle I think I would be safe in promising my hon. friend that no action would be taken on the part of the Soldier Settlement Board. But in the event of a farm being unoccupied and unseeded, it might be necessary to take some action, as would also be the case where the men had voluntarily abandoned their holdings. But proceedings to dispossess them will riot be taken.

That is hardly wide
enough, Mr. Chairman. If a man by reason of not having the money to seed his land last year, for instance, has gone out tf work and wants to continue his farm, it would not be fair to him to say, "You were not on the land last year and you are not on it this spring," when practically the board had told him that he was not going to be allowed to come back. I am asking that the board reserve to those men who have done a substantial amount of improvements and resided on their land for four or five years-fix it at the minimum of five years-the right to continue. In other words, I ask that their land should be reserved and not allotted to the Empire Settlement Board during the time within which those men should have the option of returning to their farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know whether I follow my hon. friend correctly. I do not want to make any promises that would embarrass the board in their operations, but so far as I have been able to learn there is no disposition on the part of the board to dispossess men who evince any reasonable desire to remain on the land and have some chance of making good. But to say that no action of any kind would be taken, might in some cases tie up the operations of the board. Take the case my hon. friend has just cited, if the land was not cultivated last year, and there was not much prospect of its being cultivated this year, it would be a rather serious consideration so far as that farm is concerned. On the other hand, I would be willing to go the limit in giving the soldier every chance, for I would much prefer to have him remain on the land than give it to a newcomer if the soldier has any chance at all to make good. I could not absolutely promise a cessation of operations altogether.
It is merely the principle that I want accepted.

I do not think the minister can possibly meet the request of the hon. member for Selkirk under this bill. It seems to me the point raised by him is so important, and the minister is going to be confronted with so many cases of the kind in the administration of the act, that it might be well to reserve the clause affecting it and pass on. As it appeals to me, the minister is going to run across cases of the most striking discrimination; he cannot possibly avoid it. There are going to be two or three classes. The class that the hon. member for Selkirk has in mind is this:	Men
have struggled manfully on the land against an inflated valuation, and consequently an inflated obligation, and after three or four years their hearts have grown sick with hope deferred and they have quit. They have used good judgment in doing so. They are not guilty even of bad judgment, to say nothing of bad faith. They simply saw that the land could not be paid for under the price it had to be bought at in 1919. Now that agreement is cancelled. The number of cases where the men are off the land and the agreement would be cancelled is large. It is the duty of the board when the man is off the premises to cancel the agreement and therefore the agreements would be cancelled in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred. What the hon. member for Selkirk says is this:	Are you going to
take that man who left the land simply because of the very state of affairs which is sought to be remedied by this bill, left it not because of bad judgment but of good judgment, left it not because of bad faith but of good faith to give the board the best chance to go ahead-are you going to say to that man, "You are in the cold forever, but we will invite people from England and the rest of Europe and loan them $500 to buy this land at a low' valuation." The minister sees that he will not be able to maintain that attitude, but if he leaves the bill as it is he will be in an embarrassing position.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is not suggesting that if a soldier wishes to be reinstated that be done?
It cannot be done under this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
understand my right hon. friend.

That is the point; the
minister is going to be confronted with those cases by the score.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I thought
I had made that clear when I said that where

Soldier Settlement Act
there was a cancellation of the agreement there would be no consideration.

I agree wholly with the
minister's interpretation of the act as it is. But leaving the act as it is, the minister in its administration will be confronted with a class of cases where the discrimination, the unfairness is so brutal that he will never be able to hold his position, he will have to come back to parliament and get an amendment. The class of cases presented by the member for Selkirk is a large class, and it is a class whose appeal the minister will have to answer. There is .another class where discrimination will come in, but I do not want to confuse the issue by dealing with it at the moment. I suggest to the minister that he leave this clause and take it up with the board again to see if he cannot so recast it that the board will have a discretion; or, better still, that the board will be entitled and asked to give some preference to the soldier who has worked on that land and left it solely because he saw that the obligation was too large for him to surmount.

The point I want to make
is exactly the point made by my right hon. leader in clearer language than I could make it. I understood the hon. member for Selkirk perfectly. The class of case he desires to protect is that of the man whose agreement has been cancelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Frankly, I
did not get that.

That is the man who is on
the land and is in arrears and needs a revaluation. There are scores of oases to-day where men have found it impossible to carry the burden at the price at which the land was valued when they took it over in 1919. In fact, I drew the minister's attention on the orders of the day at the opening of the session to fifty cases in the Fraser valley, where fifty families had been brought from the Old Country, to take up land that had been abandoned by soldier settlers who could not carry the load. The point is this: we consider that before one of the empire settlers is brought in to take over soldier settler land, the man who was forced to abandon that land should be given an opportunity to come in again and take over the land at a revaluation; otherwise there would be discriminar tion and unfairness to the whole class of soldier settlers who are to-day suffering from the need of revaluation. Under the act as it is drafted, those men will not be attended to. There is no obligation on the Soldier
Settlement Board to attend to them. The minister may desire that they be considered-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, no, I
quite admit that that is not in the act.

The point made by the
hon. member for Selkirk, by my leader and by myself is that those are the men for whom there is need of protection. We all know that the Soldier Settlement Board will not put a man off his land merely because he is lin arrears. We know that if a revaluation is made, and that man is making good on the land, he will not be .put off. We quite understand that. But I think the man who has been forced to abandon his land because of the burden of over-valuation should be given the opportunity to come back. The Soldier Settlement Board should be bound by legislation to reconsider the case of that man, and therefore this legislation is defective. Furthermore, I understand that the bill which is before the House is not yet printed and in our hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amendments are not there; that is the difficulty.

This is a very vital act,
one for which we have been pressing for several years past, and it involves millions of money. In my opinion it should be given the most serious consideration. I submit that we are not in a position this afternoon to consider the bill when we have not actually got it before us. We are asked to deal with a bill which the minister has read to us. I confess personally that I could not hear his explanation, and I am sure many other members could not hear and appreciate what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I should
be very glad to have the particular phase which has been brought up by the right hon. leader of the opposition, the member for Selkirk and the member for Vancouver-Burrard, discussed now at a little more length, because I have made it very clear that we are not considering the man who is off the land. If you deal with a man whose contract is cancelled, what are you going to do with the man who has paid in full? Quite a considerable number have paid up.

They did not get a
bad bargain.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not agree with you. A great many of these men have come into money; money has been left them by their friends, and notwithstanding the fact that
Soldier Settlement Act

they had a contract based on a price which undoubtedly would be reduced on revaluation, they have paid in full. How can we discriminate against a man of that class and in favour of the man who has left the land and has had his contract cancelled? I want to be generous to the soldier, but I want the House to understand that it is going to cost the country a great deal of money if we are going to take into consideration every phase of the act.

Are you figuring on
selling these lands that have been, repossessed by the Soldier Settlement Board? If it is necessary to revalue the land and reduce the price to get settlers why can Canada better afford to take a loss for the newcomer than for the soldier who has spent years upon it and wants to get it back?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know that argument is very appealing. I think my hon. friend wants to be fair.
Absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If you want to be fair, I doubt if you can draft an act for the purpose for which this act is designed and be fair to everybody. I will admit that at once, but I point out that as you begin to take into consideration various aspects of the soldier settlement scheme you take a mighty 'big contract on your hands. If you are going to be absolutely fair to every man who went on the land, you will find it is a most difficult proposition. I do not see how you are going to discriminate against the man who is on his land, who has made good, and paid the government every dollar. A considerable number have done so. He has made good, because undoubtedly he did not earn that money on the land, but got it from some other source and paid the government. Now, he is to be shut out, and you are going to deal with the man who has a cancelled contract. I do not see for the life of me how you can discriminate in that way.

The minister is abr
solutely right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I welcome
discussion.

The bill, as it is seems
to me, is founded upon a principle upon which the minister is never going to be able consistently to stand. Unless you get something that is defensible all around you cannot work it out. You will be driven from one post to another and will not know where you stand. You are quite right that if you come in with

this class you are going to be met with another class, against whom you are discriminating. Under the bill as it stands the minister is trying to be fair only to one class of soldier-the men still on the land. That is the principle of the bill. It is an attempt to help those soldiers who still, after five years are on the land, to the extent of reducing their indebtedness by the loss in land values. I do not believe the minister is ever going to be able to stand on that principle. But if he had said, ''Here, we have done all we can in general for the soldiers; the man on the land has been treated at least e^s well as the man off the land; now we are going to pass a piece of legislation to assist in settlement, in order to do for the settler what the vendor would do under the same circumstances; that is to say, where we have lands that are not paid for against which there is a heavier indebtedness than the value of the land itself, we intend to revalue those lands and reduce the debt to what the land is worth, because we know we cannot get any more an}^way"-if he had said that he would have stated a principle upon which he could stand. I admit it would not be as generous to some as the principle of the bill, but better to others and more consistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
quite follow that.

What I suggested was
that the minister might have framed his bill in such a way as to say to. all purchasers of soldier settler lands that wherever there is more money owed us than the land is worth, we are going to reduce the debt to the amount the land is worth. We do it. not because we think you owe us more; but because we cannot discriminate against the soldiers. We have done the best we can for the soldiers all over, but we know we cannot collect any more than the land is worth, just as a vendor would say to a purchaser: we would rather you got the land than somebody else outside. We would rather have you than an empire settler to whom we would have to sell the land at a lower price than that at which we are ready to sell it to you. We will reduce the price to you to a really fair basis and you can have it if you want it. If you do not want it, you do not need to take it. I fancy if the minister had framed his bill on that principle he never could have been jilted around from one point to another.
But how in the world he is going to stand in this position, I do not know. He cannot answer the class of cases presented by the hon. member for Selkirk. Those men will

Soldier Settlement Act
say to him:	We are far more deserving than
the other fellows who are hanging on to the land and who have done nothing. I have sold land to men who are quite content to sleep in a shack, stay there year in and year out, get enough to live on, never pay a cent, never pay a cent of taxes, and do almost nothing. That is the extent of their ambition. But others in a similar condition would simply say:	Well, we owe more than the land is
worth; we will get out and make a living; we will try to get on in the world. That is the class of cases presented by the hon. member for Selkirk. Will the minister say to the man who hung around and did nothing and who really owes far more than the land is worth:	We will help you, and at the same
time say to the worker, the fellow who has realized his position and, like a man of business, has got out and tried to make a living elsewhere, a more deserving man in every way:	We will not help you at all;
you can go and shift for yourself, and we will sell the land you had to an empire settler for perhaps half the amount that stands against it? The minister never in the world will stay in that position. I will tell him right now, he will be back next year, if not this session, asking for legislation to enable him to deal with that latter class of cases. After he has done this, the case he has in mind, that is of those who have paid up, will be back on him too.
Supposing you have two farms, both bought at the same price and both of equal value, one sold to "A," an excellent settler, and the other sold to "B," a laggard. "B" lets his debt accumulate. "A" goes ahead; he and his family labour and they pay off the debt. The minister says to the laggard:	We will
help you out; we will cut your debt down to a third; and he says to the man who has had ambition and who has paid off the debt on his farm:	We have got your money and we do
not care what becomes of you. That case will be hard to meet, although not as hard as those presented by the hon. member for Selkirk.
In a word, if the minister is going to stand only on the principle of helping the settler, he cannot keep this bill in its present shape; he must deal with all settlers alike. But if he stands on the principle of protecting the public treasury and of handling government property to the best advantage of the Dominion, simply giving the soldiers the preference, he has a sound answer to all comers.

The matter complained of by the hon. member for Selkirk, with whom I entirely agree, is somewhat different and was
not brought about by the bill now under consideration. The grievance was in existence before this bill was contemplated, because it is caused by the government taking salvaged farms of soldier settlers and selling them at a reduced price to British Empire settlers and to them only. That condition existed before and it will still exist even though this measure is proceeded with on the basis suggested by the leader of the opposition, namely, that of making the best of a bad bargain, which, I take it, is practically the attitude he assumes.
That is it.

I suggest that we might still deal with this measure and then deal with the other not so much by legislation as by government administration. In the past without any legislation they perpetrated the injustice complained of by the hon. member for Selkirk. That is, they took these salvaged farms and sold them at a reduced price, but they reserved them for men across the sea. The Canadian citizen, whether he was on the land or not, should have had the preference, but the government or the board made some kind of deal for British Empire settlement by which they agreed to provide so many thousand farms and they are apparently adhering to that agreement and reserving those salvaged farms for that purpose. They will not sell them to any Canadian at all; they will give the preference to a Britisher who may never have been a soldier.
The past cannot be undone; they cannot take back such of these lands as have been already resold under this settlement scheme; but they should at least, merely as a matter of administration, declare that the land-I am talking about the salvaged farms-at its reduced price will be offered first to Canadian soldiers and second possibly to Canadian citizens before it goes into the British Empire scheme. That is the weakness of that scheme. The grievance is not caused by the introduction of this bill. I would suggest that to the right hon. gentleman.

I did not say that, but the bill creates this discrimination that never can remain. I have been in governments long enough to know that if you have not an answer for a delegation who can show a gross discrimination against themselves, you will yield to that delegation.
But the discrimination was there before this bill was introduced.
No discrimination.

May I suggest also
that only 500 farms have been actually given

to British Empire settlers? It is proposed to settle 1,3C0 this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Twelve
hundred.
I am asking that that be not done in the meantime while this bill is going through.

I would
like to make a suggestion for the consideration of the minister which it appears to me might remedy the situation. To make my point clear, let me give this illustration. Supposing I was a' returned soldier who took up a farm under the board. I remained on it for four years and then I came to the conclusion that I had purchased it at such a price that I never could make good. I left it. I am now off the farm. The government decide in this bill to make a revaluation in such cases. Assuming that I come to the minister and put my case to him, saying:	I
left the farm because it was valued at 87,000; your board to-day will value it at only $5,000; I spent four years of my life on it and I would like to get the first chance to go back. In dealing with an individual case the minister will say to me:	Yes, you did
considerable work on that farm and you will get the first chance as it is now vacant. I think that is what he will tell me. -If I understand the point of the hon. member for Selkirk, he is asking the minister to extend that same principle not to one individual but to all of the class.
Opportunity.

In that way men who have made certain improvements on those farms but who, as my leader said, using their best judgment, left them, so that the farms are now vacant, can come to the government after this legislation goes through and say: Under your revaluation scheme we want to go back on our land. Who are their competitors? Their competitors are British Empire settlers, and so we ask that the government reserve those farms for some period to the former occupants. The minister suggested a period of six months, and I think that would be very fair.
I come now to the suggestion that these abandoned farms be not turned over to empire settlers or any other class of settlers coming in for a period of say four or six months, or whatever time the minister determines in his legislation, and that those soldier settlers who have abandoned them be notified that they are now available under this revaluation scheme, the time being fixed within which they must elect. If that period is fixed at six 	;	' ' I al
months, that puts me, for example, in the position that within six months I can come and get my farm back. That gives the man who has done work on that farm a preference over all others.

I have been thinking of
offering a suggestion that might be considered to advantage by the minister. It seems to me that any soldier who desired to obtain land which he had himself previously occupied, or which perhaps some other soldier had farmed, should be given the preference over a stranger, coming within our gates. The object of this scheme was no doubt originally to settle people on the land, but it was secondarily-I am not sure that it was not primarily-the intention to assist soldiers to go upon the land if they wanted to do so. I am sure the minister is anxious to further that end. Now, in view of the discussion which has so far taken place today, and in view of the suggestions which have been made, of a very sound and sane character, on behalf of those soldier settlers who may be deprived of their land if this bill goes through in its present form, I would advise the minister, with the most sincere desire to have the legislation improved, to hold up the bill temporarily in order that he may be able to consider it further with the Soldier Settlement Board to see whether some arrangement looking to the end I suggest might not be submitted by way of amendment. I have had no legal training, but I venture to think that I could frame an amendment that would meet the suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There would be no difficulty in regard to the amendment. It is a question of principle.

There would be no difficulty in framing an amendment to cover the point that has been raised but there might be some difficulty in meeting some other objection that might be involved. It would be better, I think, for the minister to take the matter up with the Soldier Settlement Board and have the bill re-drafted. If there are several branches that might be affected by the amendment, they could also be taken into consideration. I really think that the minister would do w'ell to hold up the bill for the time being and, after discussing it with the board, bring it back next week when the House would be in a better position to consider it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There would be no difficulty about amending the bill to meet the contingency raised, but we must

Soldier Settlement Act
bear in mind all the facts. Speaking from memory I think there are 500 farms that have been sold to British settlers, and in addition to these a considerable number have been sold to Canadian civilians. My hon. friends must not forget that in attempting to widen the scope of the legislation we are apt to open the door to unlimited difficulties.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I speak
subject to correction, but I do not think there was very much depreciation in the particular farms I have mentioned.

There are many
farms in which there is depreciation.

There may be some in my hon. friend's locality. But as a matter of fact the salvaged farms to date show a profit.
Mr. HAN-NESSON:	Not those sold under
the empire settlement scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am now
referring to the whole lot of them.

The minister is speaking
only of farms that have been sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but
they are a factor in the discussion. If we say to the man whose agreement has been cancelled, "Seeing that your farm is not sold we will give you an opportunity to purchase," what shall we say to the other 4 p.m. fellow from whom some civilian had bought land for less money than is paid to-day? That man would come back and tell us that had he been treated fairly he would have taken up his farm again.

Merely because a wrong
has been done to some in the past is no reason for doing a wrong to others to-day. Certain things that were wrong were done under the act in the past, and they cannot be undone, but that is no reason why we should go on injuring other soldiers whom we might treat more fairly. That is my argument for holding up the bill for the present.
Mr. STEW7ART (Edmonton):	I am not
objecting to that argument, but I want the committee to appreciate the difficulty of securing an equitable adjustment. If I could have conceived any equitable way of meeting the difficulty a year ago I would have been ready to recommend revaluation then, but the whole problem is hedged around with difficulties of all sorts. There are difficulties no matter from what angle you view it. I have no doubt that every individual member can
get up and point to some case of discrimination, and there is no lawyer in this House who in my opinion could devise a means of meeting all those cases.

The minister is referring to individual cases. I would remind him that there is a large class of cases of returned soldiers who on coming back, because of red tape or for some other reason, found it necessary to borrow money on their lands at inflated rates of interest. W7hat will the minister do with such men? These are not isolated cases; they constitute a large class.
Mr. STEW7ART (Edmonton): I agree with the hon. member.

There will no doubt be
difficulties in the application of the act but probably they will not be so great in actual practice as they appear to be in this discussion. In my judgment, the greater number of those who left the land through discouragement will not want to come back. In most cases they have had enough of hard experience to make them disinclined to return; and their equipment, too, has been sold. I doubt therefore whether there will be any applications from such men to be reinstated. At the same time, however, the bill should be so framed as to allow any such who might care to take advantage of it to do so. I felt from the outset that there would be considerable difficulty in framing a satisfactory bill if wo intended to apply the principle of absolute justice to all. That simply cannot be done. A reference to Hansard will show that as far back as 1922 the hon. member for Red Deer and myself proposed that we should consider the whole question as a new colonization scheme. Whether the principle of dealing fairly as between soldier and soldier was uppermost in the mind of the government of the day when the bill was first passed is immaterial. Whatever objection has been taken to a revaluation has been based upon the fact that we were dealing unfairly with the country. But our answer to that objection has always been that the country stands to suffer a great loss anyway and we might just as well face the situation. Bearing that in mind, may we not adopt the principle of a salvage scheme in framing this legislation? We want to make the best of what, in spite of all good intentions, has turned out to be a bad job, and I fancy that it would be just as well for us to put aside the idea of absolute justice in every case and simply consider the matter as a colonization scheme. I was severely criticized by my opponent in the last election for so describing it on one
Soldier Settlement Act

occasion, but it seems to me to be the only-practical way of dealing with the problem. Let us regard it as a colonization scheme and make the best we can of what has proved to be a bad job. If there are any men who are anxious to go back on the land under a revaluation, let us make it possible for them to do so. In any case, the number in my opinion will be small; but even if it is small let us draw up the legislation in such a way as to take care of them.

In view of the fact that some amendments have already been proposed, would it be possible between now and next Monday for the minister to appoint a small committee to revamp the bill so as to meet the views held on all sides of the House? I am sure that we all want to see the scheme made workable so as to render justice to all concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am perfectly willing to have the bill revamped, but I assumed the general opinion was that we were going to deal only with the men who were actually in residence on the land. But I have been mistaken; that does not seem to have been entirely the consensus of opinion in the House. If I get the opinion of the House there is no difficulty about preparing legislation; the difficulty is to know exactly how far everyone wants to go. I want to say very frankly that when you have thought of all the different people you want to help, you will still have a whole army which you cannot help. I ask my hon. friend again, what right has anyone to prepare legislation that will help the man who has paid up- we have all his money and he is a success- or to help the man who made a failure; through no fault of his own he is penniless; he will have difficulty in buying implements again in order to return to the land. There are two classes; if you help one you must help the other, but then are you to say to the man who has been cleaned out altogether and who has had his land sold, that you cannot do anything for him?
As you go on you will find innumerable cases which cannot be covered by legislation. I want the committee to understand clearly that I started out with the best intentions in the world of helping the men. I do not agree with the statement of my hon. friend that many of these men have just stuck there without doing anything, because most of those chaps are gone; they have been wiped out. The man we want to help is the one who has struggled and stuck and hoped that something would happen, living in penury and still wanting to stick. We might very well help that 
man now; this legislation was drafted for the sole purpose of helping him, because he is still in possession of his contract and he still feels that if he can get reasonable treatment he will continue. If we are to widen the scope I want to know how far we are to widen it, because there is no use in my spending three or four hours working away and then bringing the bill back, to find that some other member has found something else to object to. That is what I am anxious about [DOT] this afternoon; I want co know how far parliament thinks I should go with this revaluation.

We all realize there is going to be injustice done to some. The man who has paid in full can be considered later; what we are primarily interested in now is land settlement, and fair treatment to the settler. I gave this House a number of instances of men who had been put off the land only last year, or who had been told to get off. Those men have struggled for seven or eight years, and those are the men I want to protect. To-day I mailed to the minister copies of letters from men who have either been driven off their land or have been threatened with eviction. All I am asking is that consideration be given these cases where men are either living on the farm or want to stay there, having done a certain amount of improvement work. Fix a value, if you like, of $1,000 or $1,500 for the improvements; say that he must have been on the land for five years; limit it in any way, so long as the men fitted for land settlement are kept on the farms. There is an idea prevalent among the soldier settlers that other people, empire settlers and civilians, are shown a preference over these men, after they have struggled on the land for years.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is now giving me something on which I can draft legislation. If it would satisfy my hon. friend to say definitely that a man must have been in residence for five years and that he must have created improvements to the value of $1,000, we know what to do. But even so, some other hon. member will immediately present another difficulty.

I received to-day a petition signed by fifteen soldier settlers of my constituency, and it might help the situation if I read it:
Seeing that an increasing number of soldier settlers are finding it impossible to meet payments due The Soldier Settlement Board and live in a manner becoming free born British subjects, and furthermore as it appears that settlers coming from Great Britain

Soldier Settlement Act
are being given land, stock, etcetera belonging to soldier settlers at a reduction of at least 50 per cent cn the first cost to soldier settlers, these soldier settlers having been forced off the land through excess valua-t:on at time of purchase.
It is resolved that the time haa come for the government of Canada to make an immediate re-valuation, said re-valuation to be at least a 50 per cent reduction on purchase price.
It is further resolved that no soldier settlers be asked to sign a quit claim deed until the case is investigated by a party of three: first, one party appointed by the Soldier Settlement Board; second, one party appointed by the soldier settlers; third, one party appointed by The Soldier Settlement Board and soldier settler representatives. If after investigation it is shown that the inability of the soldier settler to make the payment due the Soldier Settlement Board is through no fault of the settler, he should be entited to continue on the farm.
Here is a clause which I do not quite understand.
If after investigation the settler is still forced to leave the land, he should be paid $25 for each month he has been on government land.
After the 50 per cent cut on the loan has been approved by the government all arrears should be advanced and placed over the remaining period of the original twenty-five years.
This meeting is on record demanding that these recommendations be carried out before the next Soldier Settlement Board payment is due, otherwise the majority of soldier settlers will be forced to leave the farms.
That petition is signed by fifteen of the boys who have been overseas, giving their regimental numbers. I think we should be as liberal as possible to these men who have been struggling on the land out west. In my opinion it is far better to do that than to proceed with the present scheme of giving $500 to some stranger coming to Canada, and $1,000 to another man who has been here perhaps a year or two and has become naturalized. In these latter cases the lumber merchants in the small towns trust the man with lumber for his buildings; the storekeeper trusts him until he gets his loan; the man has not had very much experience in western Canada, and becomes a failure. I think we should help our soldier settlers first, and so keep on the land the men who have had some experience and who are acquainted with conditions in western Canada.

I do not wish to go beyond the actual point being discussed. At the risk of repeating a little, let me say that I think the minister recognizes the fact that suggestions coming from this side of the House are not captious and are not intended to place difficulties in the way of the bill. As far as the soldier settlers are concerned, those acquainted with the facts know that they all regard this as a reform, if I may call it such, which is long overdue, and they are very appreciative of the efforts
being made by the minister to give them something in the way of relief. While it may not make any difference to the minister,
I may say that personally the principle of this measure commends itself very strongly to me, and I think he is endeavouring to work out some real redress for men whom everyone in this countiy wants to help.
With that preface let me say that anyone who has studied this problem realizes that it is encompassed with difficulties. You cannot possibly remove the injustice in every case. The case of a man who has paid up fully becomes a very difficult proposition. Take this case for which we are trying to provide a remedy, that of men who have put in time on farms and then left. What galls them is this: if I have put in four or five years on a farm and because the valuation was inflated I have had to leave, you now bring in a principle of revaluation and I see an empire settler or a civilian come in on my farm, under the revaluation.
It naturalljTgalls them, and I feel there is an injustice. I feel that appeals to the average man. So all we say is this, give the man who has put in time on the farm a chance.
I do not think it would be difficult to bring him under the act. It would not be remedying all injustices, but it would be providing a remedy for that class of cases, and I think the minister if he is so disposed can easily draft a clause that will give that class the first chance of farms that have not been disposed of. I would like to see such a clause inserted in the bill.

I am intensely in sympathy with the proposal of the hon. member for Selkirk, and I would strongly suggest to the minister the advisability of considering favourably some such amendment to the bill. But there does appear to me to be a difficulty; it may not be an insuperable one; I hope it- will not be, and that is the class of farm which has been abandoned by the soldier one or two years ago and has already been sold or is in the possession of somebody else. If we could get over that difficulty, I see no opposition in this House to the amendment proposed.

The bill as introduced is designed to help only one class of men, those who are still on the land and are fortunate enough to be still in debt. It does not apply to those who are unfortunate enough to have paid up. The minister said that he would like an indication from the House as to how far this bill should go. For my part, I would go the whole way. If you are
226S
Soldier Settlement Act

going to have a revaluation, then to be fair you must revalue al'l the lands, and it must apply to all classes. The man who has paid up is the easiest class of all to deal with. All you need to do in regard to him is to make a refund. His case presents no complications at all. It is simply a matter of money, and he is just as much entitled to be considered as the man who has not yet paid up. The only difference is that you have got his money, and you have not got the other fellow's. You are not going to demand full payment from the man who has not paid up, so I think you should make a refund to the man who has paid up. The only fair legislation that can be enacted is legislation that will deal with all classes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You cannot reach all classes. There are 6,000 men now who have abandoned their farms, and a fair proportion of those farms have already been sold, some of them at a reduced valuation.

speechtext: There are 1,000 who have paid up, and 6,000 who have abandoned their farms altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. Now one of those 6,000 may come to you and say: John Jones, a civilian, got my farm; I have no complaint if you create a reduction, but if you do so, you should give me the opportunity to get my farm back at that reduced value. What are you going to do in that case? It is true there will probably be only a few such cases, but undoubtedly there will be cases of that kind, and I merely mention these things to show how absolutely impossible it is to be fair all round.

It seems to me that
the case raised by the hon. member for Selkirk could be dealt with in a very simple manner by following the same course we take with regard to homestead entries. Under the present regulations any land thrown open for homesteading is eligible for entry by soldier settlers forty-eight hours in advance of the time at which civilians can file entry. It appears to me that this is not a case for legislation at all; it is simply a matter of administration, and if the minister would intimate to the committee that he would make a departmental regulation to cover the ease, I think it would meet the situation fairly well. Put all these soldier lands on the market

again, advertise them for a certain length of time, and let all soldiers who have previously held land be given an opportunity to make application, and their applications be considered before further action is taken. It seems to me that is the only fair way to deal with it. The soldier who has abandoned his land or has been evicted by the board is usually not the very best man to make a new contract with, and I am rather of the opinion that in the great majority of these cases the board would not sell to him. There are oases where they would, but I think, after all, we are making a mountain out of a molehill, because I think very few of these men will be in a position or will want to go back on the land at the present time. To meet the wishes of the committee, I think the minister might promise that some such regulations will be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend mean that he be given a second chance in the event of his exercising his homestead right? He now has a preference if he has not exercised his homestead right.

I would give him the
opportunity to make application for available Soldier Settlement Board lands.

In such a case what adjustment would you make regarding the payments the soldier had made? I hold in my hand a letter from a soldier who in addition to the grant he got from the Soldier Settlement Board paid $1,000 in cash for his land and $964 for equipment. This man claims that he is almost being driven off the land, that he is just hanging on. Suppose he is forced to leave the land, and seizes the opportunity suggested by the hon. member for Mackenzie, what adjustment would be made with regard to the money he had paid?

I cannot see that this should be taken into consideration at all. His equity has all disappeared. He has thrown up the land, he finds his money has gone, and the best thing the board can do is not to sell him that particular farm, for perhaps it is the very last farm he would want, but the board will have these lands written down to their actual value, and I assume the man would have to pay the actual value of the land.

There seems to be about as much diversity of opinion in regard to this bill as there was when this question was before the committee some years ago. When the bill was up here before, I asked for certain information regarding the number of men in each province in certain categories. I

Soldier Settlement Act
also pointed out that no bill could be successful unless some provision was made for those settlers who had paid up in full, who had perhaps borrowed the money from their friends or outside sources. They should have, in my humble opinion, exactly the same treatment as the man who is hanging on to his land by an eyelash. The minister has also failed to state to the House exactly what he means regarding whose property shall be available for revaluation. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Why not? And if so,
why should not the man who has paid up be entitled to the same consideration as the man who owes money to the department? Is the revaluation to be only to the extent of the indebtedness presently before the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

That is most absurd and unfair. If a man owes $3,000 he gets $3,000 taken off the value of his land; if he owes merely $30 he gets only $30 allowed under exactly similar circumstances. These anomalies must be considered before the bill is passed by this House. I am firmly of the opinion that any revaluation should take cognizance of conditions all the way through; that is, the man who has paid up, the man who has not paid up, and the man who has been forced off his farm either by the excessive cost of the land or by circumstances over which he had no control.

Mr. Chairman, I have not
very many men in my county affected by the provisions, of this bill, but there are some. It seems to me that there are three classes affected: Those who have paid in full and abandoned; those who have partly paid and abandoned, and those who are still upon the land.

There are
no abandonments where they have paid in full.

had left after completing their payments.

Now, why should not preference be given to every man, whether he is now on the land or not so long as he was once on the land, whether he has paid in full or in part? And why should not a period of say six months be given every soldier to apply for any lands which are vacant? I would not go any further than that,, for naturally he could only expect ito get lands which are vacant. If that was done, you would take care of all soldiers who have still a desire to go on the land. I appreciate the other difficulties respecting the seeming injustice to those who have paiid in full. I do not know whether the minister has made any effort to ascertain how much money would 'be required to carry out a law which would be fair to everyone. be very difficult to say. We estimate that under the provisions of the present act readjustment would not cost more than $10,000.000. If you were to take in all the classes mentioned it might cost $30,000,000.

are only a thousand paid up in full.
