Might I say to the minister that in the interests of the country as well as of parliament he might well take the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and redraft his bill on a different basis? The more we discuss this bill the more difficulties we see we are going to be involved in, and the more unfairness will be inflicted upon certain classes of soldiers. To my mind there was never any justification for the title of this bill. It might have been brought in as a colonization scheme or something of that sort, but it should never have been called a soldier settlement act, for you are automatically disfranchising from three-fourths to nine-tenths of our soldier settlers. Now we are going one step further and excluding from the operation of this measure those soldier settlers who have paid up in full-those who have borrowed money from their friends and put it into their land-some of whom have lost and some of whom have made good. The government have already taken, ten per cent of the value of these lands out of the soldier settlers; now they are going back to take the land itself and keep the ten per cent. How are we going to justify this and then revalue a certain number of the farms, writing down the settlers' obligations and starting them all over again? The unfairness is brought out more strikingly every way you look at this bill. I think the minister would be well advised to redraft the bill and at least remove some of these injustices that result from playing off one class of soldiers against another class, and the bill should be re-introduced under the title of a land settlement scheme. I think the minister will find that both he and the government will be in very great difficulties if the measure passes in its present form.

Has the minister given the
House the number of those who have paid for the land in full, apart from the question of arrears? For instance, a man buys a farm for $5,000, with the payments spread over a number of years, has the minister the number of those who have paid the money? I would have thought all the lands were sold on a similar plan, and that the payments would not have matured in full.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They did
not mature, but the soldier paid it.

Soldier Settlement Act
Did he get a discount?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Just to save interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know the incentive. They were all sold on twenty-five year contracts. There may have been some cases where the settler made that amount off the land. I do not believe there would be many. The settler must have got his money from some other source and applied it on the land.
I wanted to find out the number of men who have absolutely paid one hundred cents on the dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is around a thousand.

That brings up the point I raised that these men who have paid in full should have the same consideration as the other men. The minister says he does not believe the man earned the money off the land, but must have acquired it from some other source; therefore I think he is entitled to the same treatment. The hon. member from Muskoka-Ontario has raised the question of the ten per cent initial payment on the land. If the hon. member from Marquette is right and the revaluation should be made on the basis of a fifty per cent reduction, it is to be remembered that a certain percentage had been paid by these men before they went on the land in the first place. Serious consideration, therefore, should be given to the cases of those who made payments for a term of years at least and then abandoned the land.

I hope the administration of the act will be carried out in an equitable manner and that the soldier settlers will be given full justie. About seventeen thousand of these men went on the land and I am sorry that in a country like Canada they have not received more equitable treatment. Probably one hundred thousand of our returned men went to the United States, but seventeen thousand of these returned men were brave enough to settle on the land. It was a very arduous task to undertake to settle on the land, a task calling for perseverance, courage, cheerfulness, and many other estimable qualities. These men went on the land in good faith, and surely the legislation which we are now considering should be framed in such a way as to deal fairly and equitably with them. It is most desirable that there should be no red tape in the administration of this act, as there has been in the administration of other similar acts. After all is said and done, Canada has not dealt very generously with the returned men. These men are not going to live forever. They went on the land in 1919 and 1920, when conditions were not as good as they are to-day. Some of them were not farmers and could not cultivate the land, or raise any kind of crops. They had to put up with many privations, while the returned soldiers in Australia and New Zealand fared very much better; they received much better treatment from their respective governments.
I have in my hand a book published by Major Belford on Migration within the Empire, showing how the settlements were made in Australia, where they have not as much red tape as we have in Canada. There is just about as much red tape about the application and administration of this measure as there is in a case in the Supreme court. We have had enough legislation with regard to the soldiers, and I think it is time that they got their dues. Legislation has been passed, a pension board was created, but there is so much red tape that it is almost impossible for the returned soldiers to obtain justice.
The government dealt with the men who constructed the railways out west in a very different manner from that which they have adopted in connection with the soldiers who have built the empire. The railway men. were given land of all sorts and cash grants. They obtained from the government the Crowsnest pass agreement; they were given gold-bearing lands and mines simply for the asking, but here we have seventeen thousand returned men who are not treated quite so well. The government deserves great credit for what they did for the men in 1920.
Some of these men who went on the land had no experience whatever, and of course the undertaking required perseverance and courage and demanded men who were one hundred per cent efficient. Do not forget that these men fought the battles of the empire. Some of them are not farmers, and these men should be placed in the preferred class. They are not like the settlers who come from continental Europe, who are receiving better treatment from the government. The government should cut out the red tape and treat these men properly. They are just as much entitled to vested rights out west as the railway corporations who are given grants of land and money.
It looks to me as if this bill would lead to a great deal of difficulty. It calls for valuations and revaluations. Now, who is going to pay the costs incurred by the soldiers when they have to produce witnesses and prove their claims? New Zealand and Australia led the
Soldier Settlement Act

way in showing this country how to deal with returned men. It was hard enough before the war to get the men to go on the land, and the great difficulty now is in. getting men to come out here from England, Ireland and Scotland. I read in the Toronto Star a statement that the government of Canada were going to cut off further immigration of farm workers or something to that effect.
The government should not conduct this act as a mortgage company would a foreclosure. They should be free, easy and elastic in their dealings and the administration should be a little easier than it has 'been in the past. As these men are not going to live forever, the government should give them additional cash. They are spending money to bring in immigrants from continental Europe. They should go a little further than they are going now. Under this -bill the returned men must go to the district superintendent, who will consider their application and the material in support of it and make report and recommendation to the board. Application to revaluation must be made to the district superintendent of the Soldier Settlement Board. They must go to him, and the application must be supported by affidavit, setting out the original purchase price of the land and the value of improvement effected since the [DOT] establishment of the settler thereon, by written statement of the settler setting forth his belief as to present value of the land, his reasons therefor, and so on. With all those provisos, who is going to present the case of the returned soldier? As in the case of the act regarding pensions, there should be some other way of allowing soldiers to deal adequately with their claims. There are too many technicalities in connection with this matter, and by the time we have got to the end of it many returned men will have given up their land as a bad job and will think they are well rid of it. They have been frozen out of the -land in many cases through no fault of their own. I hope the minister will see to it that those who are appointed to administer this legislation will be free from political bias, and that they will endeavour, as regards these 17,000 men who fought for Canada in continental Europe, to re-establish them on the land- under a better and more reasonable agreement by which they will have some opportunity to make good.

I am in sympathy with the principle of this bill. I know it is difficult for the minister to draft a bill that will meet all phases of the question, but I wish to impress upon him the desirability of giving men who have, from whatever cause it may

be, temporarily abandoned their land, an opportunity of again taking possession of it under the revaluation scheme proposed in the bill. The feeling seems to be general amongst returned men on the land that they are being discriminated against in favour of men coming in under the empire land settlement scheme; we have all received letters to that effect. I think the purpose of the bill is to help returned men who are still on the land, and I would like to see it extended to help those who, as I said before, are not now upon the land but have temporarily abandoned it because they found it necessary to make a living for themselves and their families in some other profession. They have no doubt spent a large portion of their lives in an effort to make good on the land, and because conditions have been against them and made it impossible for them to succeed, they have been forced to leave the land for a time. I would ask the minister to see that the bill is amended in some way to give these men a chance to come back and settle on the land under the present revaluation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Toronto Northwest said that he had read in the press that immigration was being stopped. The only difficulty we are facing at the moment arises out of the arrangement that was made a year ago when we had a great number of these farms throughout Canada salvaged, some of them unoccupied, but held by the crown and therefore non-taxable. I am being bombarded daily for the payment of taxes on these lands, and I have written the municipalities and municipal officials saying that we were going to make a special effort this year to clean this up in order that the lands might go back into the taxable category. Having that in mind, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), when he was in charge of the Department of Immigration, entered into an arrangement with the British Overseas Settlement Board whereby the latter provide $1,500 of British money to each settler for the purpose of buying stock and equipment. These things were done with the best intention in the world. These lands have been inspected. It is not fair to say that civilians were denied the right to purchase them if they wanted to do so, but they were not purchasing them and an effort was made to colonize them by people from Great Britain. An agreement was entered into to bring out 3,000 families. Five hundred families arrived last year and we hope to establish 1,200 more this year. Arrangements have been made to bring out

Soldier Settlement Act
at least 1,000 families. They have passed inspection and I am told 300 of them have already arrived here. Hon. members opposite are asking me to hold up 2,000 farms until this matter is settled. I am mentioning these things merely to show them the difficulties we are facing in the matter.
The government has other land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have no lands we own, and as under this scheme we have to provide the land, we would have to go out and buy it.
The government has brought in a bill to provide new land for settlers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a different scheme. These are all improved lands on which these families expect to go and the government of Canada is under agreement to provide the land. I am not criticizing the suggestions of hon. gentlemen opposite, nor am I putting this forward as a reason why the soldier should not have the first opportunity to purchase. I am simply telling hon. gentlemen some of the difficulties I am faced 'with as minister.

That scheme would not be in
conflict with the suggestion made, because-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If we adopt the suggestion made by hon. members opposite, it means that no settlement of salvaged land can take place until we have revalued them and the soldier who has abandoned them or has been put off has an opportunity to re-purchase.

The minister has
made his revaluation on turning the land over to the Soldier Settlement Board. All these lands were revalued by the board before the allotment was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I want to
get the suggestion clearly in mind because it is important that we should understand one another. I understand it means this:	Take
the 1,200 farms, for example, that are now practically under agreement for settlement. We say: We have reduced this farm by $500 or $1,000, if you wish, and we write to the man who abandoned it or whoever owned it previously, if he had been on it for five years and had been a reasonable settler, and we say to him: Do you want this farm? If he refuses, then the farm goes into the category for settlement by someone else.
That is right.

If no allotment has been made, these lands will be available to soldiers who have been on the land and abandoned it. That gives the man a preference only for a period of time so far as available lands are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The man
has only an opportunity of going on the land which he formerly occupied?

No. The suggestion made
from many quarters of this House is that it should be opened wider than that and that any soldier who has been on the land and has abandoned it for any reason should be given a preference for a period of time to settle on any lands which are still available with the revaluation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our difficulties would be widened by doing that. We would have to advertise the land. We are left open to criticism if we do not advertise it for a month or six weeks. We do not know what man may apply. It is quite easy to deal with the man who formerly occupied the land if we know where he is.

That would not be any good, because in many cases the land he was on has been allotted under this scheme and resold to somebody else. There would be discrimination in that way. As regards advertising, one or two insertions in the leading papers of Canada, merely giving some information regarding the provisions of the bill and telling the soldiers that if they so desire they may still get land at the revaluation, would be sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the committee can readily understand the number will be reduced almost to the minimum for this very reason:	No one will suggest that
the government should again provide loans for the individual with which to buy stock and equipment. He would have to provide for himself in that respect and it would be a tremendous handicap. Formerly he was established with both stock and equipment. I should like my hon. friends to confine it to the individual who owned the land, because in that event the difficulties would be reduced very appreciably. If you make it wider than that we shall have to keep the lands unoccupied for a considerable time.
Mr. BOY'S:	There is where the minister
misunderstands me; I did not suggest that. You would advertise and get an application for certain property, and if that property had since been sold or allotted to someone else it would of course be no longer available. But



Soldier Settlement Act
you could inform the applicant to that effect and tell him that you had a number of other lots to offer.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is a
serious difficulty.

Where the revaluation
has been made and' the man has been continuously on the land for a number of years, having made certain payments, I think that some compensation commensurate with the revaluation should be given him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
going too far.

I would suggest that the
minister, in order to meet the difficulty, might strike out of paragraph 68-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the committee will give me a clear idea of what it would like me to do I think my hon. friend might leave the drafting of the bill to me.

I am not making an
amendment but only offering a suggestion. I would suggest that the following words be omifted:
-whose agreement with the board has not been terminated or rescinded and who has not repaid his indebtedness to the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would absolutely refuse to accept that. I am going to deal with the matter on definite principles; 1 will not foe left in the air with a bill that might mean anything or nothing. I want to know precisely what classes are to foe dealt with, and if I can get the consensus of opinion of the committee I shall be in a better position to go ahead.
Only the soldier who has taken land under the act is being dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will find that he is doing a great deal more* than that. First we deal with the men who are on the land1 and in ownership, and now my hon. friend wants me to extend that to the men whose lands have been salvaged. If I understand the views of the committee, we are first of all to notify the 5 ip.m. former occupant, the soldier who formerly had the land, and no one else, that if he so desires he can within two months get the land back at the revaluation, provided he can re-establish himself. There are 500 men who have paid in full and 500 whose lands will foe revalued, and if the board should find that these have paid an excessive price for their land they would be reimbursed accordingly.

I do not know whether
the minister contemplates doing that or not, but really I should not care to make myself popular by advocating that. I do not think the minister can do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
discussed the discrimination that would arise, as against others, from dealing with the man whose contract had been cancelled and whom I have described. If we gave him consideration how could we avoid dealing with the man who had paid an excessive price for his land? If we did not deal with that man, would there not be a discrimination against him?

If the minister proceeds on the principle of helping a certain class of soldiers to get their land back, then he will continue in the dilemma in which he finds himself now. He will be driven from that class to another and from the second to a third class, and so on, on the ground that if he did a favour to class A he must treat class B equally. The minister need not think that he will ever escape without getting to the last soldier who bought land even to the 500 to whom he has referred They will have a claim in equity which he will never be able to answer. The minister, before pressing the bill further, ought to review in his mind the suggestion I made previously. He cannot maintain this present position, and I have no doubt he will later on get into further complications and a tremendous liability if he continues extending the principle on which the bill is based in this form. Suppose he says to the soldier: "We are not proceeding with any new scheme of largesse or of assistance but we recognize that in the disposition of government property you ought always to have first choice, and we will prefer youi to another. But we do not propose to launch on a new scheme of more help out of the treasury. Here we are, however, with a mass of lands on a great proportion of which there is more money owing than we can possibly collect, inasmuch as the lands are not worth it. Now, we are going to do what any other reasonable vendor looking after his own interest would do; we are going to reduce the value of the land to what the man can get out of it. And we are going to do so in order to protect the interests of Canada and conserve public property."
If the minister does this he will never have to answer the man who otherwise might take this view:	"Here I owe only $1,000 on this
land. The valuation shows that it is worth $2,000, but I paid $1,000 more for it than

Soldier Settlement Act
I should have paid. You must therefore cancel that debt." Should the minister cancel that debt of $1,000 he never in the world could answer the fellow who had paid in full. The minister would not have cancelled that $1,000 in the interests of the people in the country; he would, in cancelling it, merely have given another grant to that soldier. But if he gives such treatment to that particular man, he will have to extend it to all the rest. With the man whose indebtedness is no more, is indeed less, than the worth of the land, the minister need not deal at all. If however he says that only in cases where he cannot collect that debt, for the reason that it is greater than the value of the land, shall it be his policy to treat with the soldier, in the interests of the country and not on any pretence of distributing a grant to certain classes of men, his position will be sound. I hope the minister follows me. I think he does, and I repeat that he can never frame a bill to meet this complicated situation unless he abandons the principle he is now pursuing- in good faith, I am sure-and adopts the other one which I have suggested and which can be defended to anyone. The principle at present being followed cannot in this limited application be defended and it will merely carry the minister from one post to another, until finally he will find himself under the necessity of extending the same treatment to everbody, right down through the list. To every one of them, their heirs at law, even to those who do not need it, he will have io give an equal measure of benevolence out of the treasury of the Dominion.

How would the amount
of relief under the scheme proposed by my hon. friend compare with the amount under this bill?

It would be less in one
direction for this reason: all these cases where the amount owing is equal to or less than the value of the land would be eliminated. Under the present scheme the minister has to go into every one of these cases, and if the man paid an excess value equal to or greater than the amount owing, the debt is cancelled although the government could have collected. That class will be eliminated, saving the treasury many millions of dollars, but the class mentioned by the hon. member for Selkirk will be taken care of on the principle that we have this plan and we will give the men who had it before, the preference. I would be willing to trust the minister with that. Some regulation might be devised generally defining his duty, but not in the form of an 14011-145i
injunction over which he cannot step. The principle could be laid down and preference given to those who had the land before.
Supposing the farm had been sold to somebody else?

Then you could not do anything but you are still in a strong fortress; you could never be attacked because you do not pretend to be doing this as a new scheme for the soldier; you are preserving government property-giving him the preference on sale.

In that way, would you not create another discrimination? There are twro classes, one whose land has been sold and the other whose abandoned land has not been sold. There would be a distinct discrimination against the man whose land has been sold.

Yes, but that has already been created; we are not doing that by this bill. Wherever there is land to be sold we will give the soldier the preference, and the minister should not be tied by very definite restrictions. We will give the soldier the preference as long as we can, without injury to the public interest, but beyound that we do not pretend to go. The whole principle is to properly administer the property of the people of Canada.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.
Do I understand that he would reduce the price to the present value of the land utterly regardless of what the soldier has already paid?
I would only deal with those cases where there is more owing on the agreement than the land is worth.

If a man bought a farm for $5,000 and paid $1,000, and the farm was to-day worth only $3,000, in his case you would have to wipe out $1,000. In the case of another man who bought a similar farm for the same price and paid nothing, you would wipe out $2,000.
Yes, just as my hon. friend would do if he were the vendor instead of the government, because it would be the best thing in his own interest and he would not pretend to do anything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

In the reconsideration *of the bill would the minister assure the House that no further lands will be allotted to the Empire Settlement Board until the details of this plan are worked out?

speechtext: I am in this difficulty, that people are being placed at the present time on some of the 1,200 farms mentioned.

Mr: STEWART (Edmonton):	But if we
follow the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the opposition we will confine this to one class only, men wlho owe more money on their land than the land is worth. speechtext: Yes, quite.

If the minister still adheres to his resolution to help the returned soldier still on the land I would like to point out a phase of the situation which has not been mentioned this afternoon. Certain returned1 soldiers are in arrear in their payments and cannot at present meet their indebtedness. They are being asked by the board to assign what they have left of last year's crop, and to also assign all of this year's crop. That is a very discouraging situation and it will certainly force more men to abandon their
[Mr. Stevens.l
farms this spring, because if a man is going to be farced to assign all his crop to the board, how is he to live during the summer months, or until the next year? It will increase the abandonments by men who have stayed five or six years on the land. If I understand human nature at all, a man who has spent five or six years on a farm without making a success of it is not going to be very anxious to go back on the land again. Only the man who has still an interest in the land, who possibly left his family there, or who only temporarily abandoned it, will go back, but he should certainly be given an opportunity of re-possessing (that land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I hope the
committee quite appreciates the idea of the right hon. leader of the opposition, because it does reduce the difficulties tremendously. I was trying to cover a much wider field, and I do not deny for a moment all the d-ifficulti.es with which this proposition is bristling. The proposition of the right hon. leader of the opposition, however, confines it to men whe to-day, at the present moment, owe -more tc the government or to the Soldier Settlement Board than the land is actually worth, and *that is the only class to be dealt with. I want the committee to understand exactly what that means; it cuts out the man who has paid in full; it cuts out the man who has reduced his indebtedness below the value of .the land to-day even by only $200 or any small amount; it cuts out these parties altogether. They would get no consideration under this measure suggested, which would only deal with the man who is not a good, solvent risk for the government. That, in effect, is what it means.

I would like to ask the
.minister a question which I should have asked the leader of the opposition, had he been in the House. In a case where a soldier owed, say, $500 on land, but $1,000 on chattels, and was in straitened circumstances and in danger of losing his farm, following the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, he would1 be given consideration for the $500 only. He would Still owe the $1,000 on his chattels and would stand a good chance of being driven off the land. In that case it seems to me the government would' still run a considerable risk of losing the settler, and losing as well the $1,000.

Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I asked
that question myself because I wanted to be dear about it. If I followed the leader of the opposition carefully his answer was no, simply the land-and the land, of course, includes the buildings; stock is not to be taken into consideration. In that case ithe soldier would have to abandon his farm, I presume. I confess that the suggestion of the leader of the opposition appeals to me very much, because it will save the country a great deal of money.
The bill will be of very little use in that case.

Mr. Chairman, I have here
a petition signed by 469 residents in the constituency of Macdonald. The object sought is explained in the heading of the petition, which reads as follows:
We, the undersigned, do hereby place ourselves on record as being in favour of the consolidation of the soldier settlers' debt to date, including tax arrears, and that a reduction of not less than fifty per cen be made of the amount of the total consolidation thus computed, and we will support the efforts of 'the soldier settlers to obtain his redress.
The petition is accompanied by a letter which I shall read to the committee, because the petition has been very largely circulated over the whole district. The letter reads:
Sir,
In re Soldier Settlers' Lands
On the 25th of February, 1926, there met in Carman, at a largely attended meeting, a number of the soldier settlers of the district, who had purchased lands through the soldier settlers' board.
This meeting was the outcome of the increasingly arduous position in which the majority of the settlers now find themselves; the situation i^ beyond doubt well known to you, and may briefly be described as follows:
Owing to the inflated price of land which existed at the time when the majority purchased, followed immediately by an almost unprecedented slump in the selling power of farm produce, followed at a later date by a sharp decrease in land values, which is continuing to-day, the average soldier settler finds that he has now accumulated against him such a volume of arrears, which coupled with the amount still owing by the purchaser as the purchase price of his land, makes his position untenable, and it is felt that the position of the average settler is hopeless, unless some alleviation is forthcoming.
The meeting above mentioned was addressed by several civilians, i.e. other than settlers, amongst them being Reeve Armstrong of Dufferin municipality and Councillors Provo, Murray and Metcalfe, and the meeting passed the following resolution.
"We the undersigned do hereby place ourselves on record as being in favour of the consolidation of the soldier settlers debt to date, including tax arrears, and that a reduction of not less than 50 per cent be made of the amount of the total consolidation thus computed, and we will support the efforts of the soldier settlers to obtain this redress."
A committee was formed, and the above was circulated in the form of a petition in the districts of Carman, Roseisle, Haywood, St. Claude. Somerset and
Treherne, meetings being held at a number of these points, and it has been the experience of those circulating the petition that the entire community, with less than 1 per cent of those approached, is in favour of the redress asked being granted.
At the risk, Sir, of wearying you with facts which doubtless are well known to you, this branch of the Soldiers Settlers' Association desires to emphasize to you that unless this redress is forthcoming, the large majority of our soldier settlers will be forced to give up the struggle, and, instead of being settled on the land, will drop to the status of men without homes and without those ties which it is believed are essential to the building up of the west.
Another point which we would with respect draw to your attention is that as each soldier settler is forced to bandon his farm or is evicted by the board, a revaluation takes place, and the land, with the permanent improvements added and charged against the settler, thus revalued, is sold to an incoming settler, at a price which in many cases is 50 per cent and in seme cases, more than 50 per cent, less than the amount which was owing by the settler with the improvements added; if the loss has to come, and from the policy of the board and the current price of land, it would appear inevitable that a loss will accrue, it is felt and urged that the soldier settler should in all fairness receive the benefit in the reduction of land values.
t As you, Sir, are without doubt aware, a bare reduction in the amount of the purchase price now outstanding will not in itself save a large number of our settlers; they owe such an accumulation of arrears, which, if left in status quo, even if the future debt be reduced, will so clog and hamper the efforts of the settler, that he cannot hope to meet his obligations, or if meeting them, will prevent the necessary development of his farm owing to shortage of working capital.
The legislature of Manitoba and that of Alberta have expressed themselves in favour of some redress being granted; Mr. J. R. Love, U.F.A. member in the House at Edmonton, on March 16th drawing attention to the condition of the soldier settlersi in the Wain-wright district, stated that of 37 settlers, 19 had been forced to quit.
Meetings in support of the movement have been held at Deloraine, Carman, Swan River, Somerset, Treherne, and Deepdale in Manitoba, and in many points as far as Dewdney, B.C. and from Deepdale, Manitoba, there is going a petition to the right hon. the Prime Minister and Mr. W. J. Ward, M.P. The petition from Deloraine has for some time been in the hands of Mr. J. Steadman, M.P., for Souris, and to you, Sir, we beg to submit a petition signed by 469 persons in this district, supporting the legislation asked for by the soldier settlers.
It is felt that all money expended by or on behalf of a settler by the board, i.e. such as the cost of breaking advanced on charge to the settler, and paid by the board should be added to the purchase price of the land in computing the amount of the settlers total outstanding liability on the land; the tax arrears should, it is submitted, be also taken into consideration in arriving at the total debt, and added thereto; if the soldier leaves the land or is ejected therefrom, the land on being re-vested in the board ceases to be liable for taxes until re-sold, and if the assistance is not directed towards the reduction of tax arrears, these arrears will be sufficient to act as a dead weight borne by the settler and a severe handicap; it is indeed felt by very many settlers that it is most vital that in computing the total debt, there should be added to the outstanding capital debt, the arrears both of taxes and past due payments. The revaluation granted in 1925 on settlers' live stock will afford an illustration

Soldier Settlement Act
on this point that revaluation averaged about $150, but taken from the capital debt only; this reduction of $150, divided over a period of say, 25 years, is of little material assistance, whereas had this been deducted directly from arrears, the assistance would have been most beneficial.
The petitions forwarded to you, Sir, are sent in the fervent hope that you may do what is in your power to assist in the passing at the present legislature, such legislation as will, in common justice, alleviate the present situation, and will assist in keeping on the land a type of citizen which Canada can ill afford to lose from her agricultural community;
We feel that in approaching you as the hitting member for Macdonald, we are taking the right step, knowing full well that you with your personal knowledge of farming conditions are in close touch with the situation as it exists to-day, and are conversant with the whole matter, and we trust that our movement will receive your support.
I would ask the minister what he thinks about consolidating all the soldier settlers' debts, including tax arrears and the expense of breaking, and spreading the payment over a period of years. Will the bill make provision for any assistance of that kind?

To put the

That concretely is what the leader of the opposition suggested. Of course that suggestion is confined to land only; it does not cover stock and equipment.
Of course, that is the intention of the bill anyhow.

speechtext:
Yes. Now,
the bill as drafted provides for what the leader of the opposition has suggested; but he confines it absolutely to the men on the land, to those in possession; those are the only cases to be dealt with, all the others are to be shut out. I am quite prepared to deal with the suggestion of the hon. member for Selkirk that where a soldier has occupied a farm, and that farm has been salvaged and a reduction in value made either by the board or by the committee that will function later, the soldier should be given an opportunity to go back on his farm at the reduced price. In that case would he be

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend has raised another difficulty. I would not care to give an answer to his question offhand. After all, I am trying to meet the objection raised by the soldiers themselves, "Had you done this for me I could have continued." There is something in what my hon. friend says, but I shall have to consider it carefully before giving him an answer. May I say that that contingency could easily be arranged for in the present bill?

Soldier Settlement Act
Now, the difference between the proposal contained in this bill and that suggested by the leader of the opposition is that the bill would give consideration to every man who is still on the land, whether his indebtedness is more than the value of the land or whether it is less. The restriction we put on is that if he gets a reduction of $1,000, and he owes the board only $700, we would not pay that $300 to him. He would simiply pay out his $700 and get his title deed. The bill is wider in that respect inasmuch as we deal with all the soldier settlers instead of confining its operation simply to the class who owe more than the amount I have referred to. Speaking casually, I cannot believe that it would entail a great deal more money than the scheme proposed by the right hon. leader of the opposition, but I admit at once that the difference between the two plans does put the government in a much stronger position with respect to claims that might come from every quarter, such as have been raised so prolifically this afternoon, because under the plan suggested by the leader of the opposition we could confine ourselves simply to the protection of the government's interests, not the soldiers' at all. That is the main point of difference. Under our plan we are taking into consideration to some extent soldier settlement. Outside of that I am bound to say at the moment-I may change my mind on further deliberation-'that our bill will better meet the situation than any other suggestion we have yet had this afternoon. Of course, I may be prejudiced in favour of this bill. Certainly I am not going to argue for a moment that it will remove all discrimination, I doubt if any bill could accomplish that, but in being fair to the government and fair to the soldiers I think the provisions of this measure pretty well meet the situation. I am speaking of course particularly with respect to the classes that will be considered under the bill.

Mr. Chairman, as I told the minister, I did not hear the remarks of the leader of the opposition to which he has referred, but I do know that all the members on this side of the House-and they are largely returned soldiers-all took the same attitude, and I am quite sure still adhere to it, as that which the minister describes as the suggestion of the hon. member for Selkirk. In other words-

speechtext: I say so still.

All right. As a returned soldier, I do not want to see the scope of the bill restricted. I am sure that that is the opinion of every returned soldier on this side of the House, and there are at least twenty. Soldier Settlement Act

speechtext:
On behalf
