or three thousand dollars a year towards the holding of a convention for the preservation of life at sea, but the money is not taken out of this vote.

I have a suggestion tc
make to the minister. We have a very valuable navy, consisting of a few trawlers and torpedo boats, which most of the time, I understand, are lodged in a boathouse down in Halifax. Indeed the member for Northwest Toronto (Mr. Church) suggested they were stored in a garage. Why should not these boats be used for this service? It seems to me that it would be the best purpose to which they could be put. The minister might pass on my suggestion to his colleague, the Minister of National Defence.
Is this work done by contract, or how?

It is usually done by our
own divers, but in very important cases we have it done by contract.

Do you keep the divers all the time?
Mr .CARDIN: One diver. He does this work.
Did you let any contracts last year?
No.
The work was all done by this one diver?
Yes.
So the amount expended was all paid to him?

Not only to him; he has
to get other men to help him.

What about the removal
of obstructions in navigable rivers? I am interested in the river St. John, which is navigable for some 84 miles from its mouth. Very frequently navigation is obstructed by sunken logs. Is the removal of such obstructions paid' out of this vote?

Yes.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
How much work was done on the St. John river last year?
None at all.

Why not? There is never a season when it is not necessary to remove snags from that river. I have heard complaints from St. John river captains that the work has not been done recently. Under the old government the work was let every year to one of the tug-boats companies. I asked about the item a few years ago and was told the service was done very efficiently by a certain company, but I was never able to find out the name of that concern. I should like to know what work has been done since the navigation season of 1901.

I have no information that any work has been done on the river St. John. We have no record of any complaints having been made of the nature mentioned by my hon. friend. Possibly the work to which he refers has been done in years gone by by the Department of Public Works.

That is what I was going
to suggest.

The owner of the
steamer that plies between St. John and Fredericton writes me that his boat has grounded two or three times during the past season. Would the work of keeping the river safe for navigation come under the Public Works department?
If my hon. friend will be kind enough to send me the letter I will make the necessary investigation, and if the work does come under our jurisdiction, I shall be quite ready to have it attended to.
I think dredging comes *under the Public Works department. I hope the minister will give the matter attention.
Most decidedly.
If this is the item under which the department in previous years has paid for removing snags from the St. John river, I hope something will be done this .season along the same lines.
We have never performed *any work of this kind; this work is under the jurisdiction of the Public Works department.
This item also *applies to the Great Lakes?
Yes.
Does the same amount each year, $5,000, take care of the removal of snags everywhere, or is this item simply for salaries?

This applies really to the removal of sunken vessels which have become obstacles to navigation. It does not apply to the dredging of navigable waters, which is attended to by the Public Works department. We only look after exceptional cases.
' Mr. ANDERSON (Halton): It would be interesting to know whether any obstructions along the Great Lakes were removed during 1923-24, for I notice the vote is the same for each year.
The only case I have is the removal of an obstacle in the St. Clair river last year.
I would have thought that if the vote was for the removal of snags from navigable waters it would- vary from year to year. Why is the same amount asked for every year?

We never know how much will be required for this work, so we follow the practice of asking for $5,000, which for a number of years has been found sufficient to meet any requisitions for the removal of obstructions. We have nothing definite upon which we can base our estimate.
That amount is expended every year?
No, it is not entirely expended every year.

Can the
minister tell me what amount was expended in removing the sand and gravel at the point where the waters from lake Huron enter into the St. Clair river, and the number of yards that were removed?
My information is that this is not under our jurisdiction.
Does the minister tell me that the obstructions to navigation at the point where the waters of lake Huron enter the St. Clair river are not under the control of this government?
They might be under the control of the department of Public Works.
What obstructions did the department remove from the river St. Clair?

We removed a steamer, the Wm. H. Wolfe, which was wrecked and abandoned.
Supply-Marine and Fisheries
What did it cost to remove the steamer?
The cost was $1,654.
Could the minister tell me what dredging, if any, was done, or what obstructions the department removed from the river Thames between Wal-laceburg and Chatham?

We performed no such
work.
No dredging was done by the department?
No, not by our department.
I suppose it would be the Public Works department that removes obstructions in those rivers.
The dredging is done by the" Public Works department. My department is looking after the dredging of the St. Lawrence ship channel only.
And the removal of snags?
Yes.
In what year was that removal made?
Last year.

Why is it that the
minister's department has charge of the dredging of the St. Lawrence and not of the other rivers?

Prior to fifteen or twenty years ago the St. Lawrence ship channel was under the control of the Department of Public Works, but there was a change; the St. Lawrence channel was transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. If I remember correctly it was during the time that Hon. Mr. Prefontaine was minister of Marine and Fisheries.
What were the reasons?

I do not know what the
reasons were at that time.
The minister does not know the reasons now.
I do not know why they did it.
Why is it not retransferred to the Public Works department, to make it uniform?
That might be a subject of consideration in the remodelling of the department.

Is it not a fact that the transfer of the dredging of the channel of the St. Lawrence from the Public Works to the Marine department has been the cause of great expense to the public, on account of the overhead involved ? The Department of Public Works has a complete outfit of dredgers, superintendents, and so on, and the transfer of this dredging from the Marine department to the Public Works has necessitated a duplicate system of overhead which is very costly to the country. If the minister wants to make a name for himself he will retransfer this dredging to the department of Public Works. The reason why it has been retained in the Marine department, I imagine, is that the St. Lawrence channel is under the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and of course having charge of this dredging magnifies the importance of the department and gives them more money to spend in Quebec, from which province for many years the minister of Marine and Fisheries has come. I suggest that if the minister wants to save the country a considerable amount of money he will do away with this duplication of overhead in the dredging service, and vest all that service either in his department or in the Public Works department. Let us save a little money on the dredging.
Does the work on the St. Lawrence ship channel come under the engineer of the Public Works department, or is there an engineering department in the Marine and Fisheries?
We have an engineering department looking after the work we are performing. There is a vote regarding that which will be considered later.

Does this item
apply wholly to the obstruction of navigable waters?
Yes.

I have in mind the state of affairs in Port Arthur, where we have plenty of derelicts which poke their noses above water. We call it the graveyard. It is an eyesore to the community. Has the .Marine department any control over that?
That would come under the jurisdiction of the Public Works department. We have the same thing in the Richelieu river, in the constituency I represent.
I wish the minister would see that the other department looks after this graveyard in Port Arthur and gets the obstruction cleared up. It is an unsightly place.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
Inspection of live stock shipments, $4,000.

This proposed appropriation is to provide for the inspection of ships carrying live stock to European ports, to see that they are properly fitted up and equipped in accordance with the provisions of the live stock act. The act provides that ships carrying live stock cannot clear from any port without a government certificate.
How many cubic feet do you allow per animal?

I must admit that the
legulations are rather complicated and rather long. I see, for example, that cattle carried on third deck must in all cases have a space of two feet eight inches in width and eight feet in length. For fat cattle earned on the upper deck there must be a space provided of two feet six inches clear in width by eight feet in length, and not less than six feet three inches in height.
Can you say whether there is any marked superiority in those new cattle shipping boats-I think it is the Jensen line- which have been put into commission recently, compared with the old system?

We have no exact information as to the advantages of the new system. The only information we have is that it provides for carrying cattle on five decks instead of three. The results are satisfactory, but we cannot say whether there has been any improvement over the other system.
What are the general provisions for ventilation and at what temperature are the cattle kept?

This is part of the report that has been made:
The system of ventilation arranged is ample for the requirements as set out by the British Ministry of Agriculture.
In liie compartments where the change per hour is slightly under ten, the loss in efficiency can be attributed to:
1.	The zero conditions prevailing at the time the tests were made, one of the fans being frozen.
2.	Lack of steam pressure at intervals, and
3.	The storage of fodder by the stevedores in every available space, irrespective of the location of the air supply and exhaust ducts, the free circulation of air in certain compartments being badly obstructed.
With higher temperatures at sea, steadier steam pressures, and consumption of the fodder during the voyage, conditions would be improved.
A survey of the four lower compartments aft during Sunday afternoon after the cattle had been two days on board showed the atmospheric conditions to be excellent.
Hon. gentlemen will understand that the matter is complicated.

What are the regulations in regard to shipping store cattle-that is cattle under 1,000 pounds-on these vessels? Are five being put in "four" space and if so what is the size of the space-two feet eight, or two feet six?

I am afraid my hon. friend is asking about a matter with which he is more conversant than I am. Probably he is asking for something that he already knows. It is rather hard for me to find it in the long list of regulations which I have before me.
I am asking for information. It is overcrowding cattle to put them in a space two feet six inches wide. It is not fair to put five cattle in space for four, giving each only two feet six.
We have two inspectors in Montreal, one in St. John and one in Quebec.

I have been wondering why this appropriation comes under the Depart^ ment of Marine and Fisheries. Logically speaking I think it should come under the purview of our friend the Minister of Agriculture, who has taken a great interest in this matter. It pertains to the safe passage of cattle and their arrival in a proper condition in the Old Country. Has this always been under the Department of Marine and Fisheries?
Yes.
Why?
Probably the idea is that the Department of Marine and Fisheries is dealing more directly with steamboat inspection.
Has the minister seen the results of any inspection that has taken place of the shipment of cattle from Canadian ports?
We are not making an inspection of the cattle. We inspect only the fittings which are placed on the ship.

Has the result of the work
of those inspectors been to bring about changes for the better in regard to the shipment of cattle?

The idea was to bring about better results but the inspectors we have are not interested at all in the cattle. They inspect only the fittings upon the vessels in order to ascertain whether or not they comply with the regulations.
Supply-Marine and Fisheries
During the inspection has any change in the fittings ever been made upon the recommendation of the inspectors?
Numerous changes have been made.
To whom do the inspectors report? If five cattle are put in space for four, do they get the standard two feet eight inch space they should have? '

Perhaps I could
supply the information. If animals are under
1.000	pounds, five are put in a stall; if over
1.000	pounds, four are put in a stall. With respect to the first report we have had from our inspectors who accompanied the first consignment by this specially equipped boat, the results have been quite satisfactory as regards the cattle. Of course the first shipment was made under very difficult circumstances owing to the storm, about which my hon. friend knows; but notwithstanding the arduous voyage the animals had they came through with less shrinkage than any cattle on any other boat that was on the Atlantic at the same time. This was due to the better facilities for taking care of the animals during the storm through which they were passing, and their increased comfort during the voyage; although there was not complete satisfaction because it was the first shipment and certain difficulties were experienced which they had not anticipated. They had a shortage of coal and they had to slow up the boat to six knots an hour, so that the voyage took several days longer. But in spite of all those difficulties this cattle shipment came through better than any other boat that carried cattle during the same period. We have no report as to the second boatload, except a wireless as to its arrival on the other side. Everything seems to indicate that the five-deck boat has come to stay. Some changes have been made in regard to ventilation after the experiences of the first trip. The facilities as regards cleaning the animals have been improved. They provide for taking them out every day. According to the report that has been submitted to us, the facilities will have to be considerably enlarged to provide for the proper cleaning of the quarters. Otherwise the necessary sanitation will have to wait until the arrival of the ship on the other side. The first attempt at improving the facilities has been successful and the second trial promises an equally satisfactory result.

What is the sense of
inspecting the hygienic surroundings of the animals when the animals themselves are not examined for disease?

The vessels are
equipped to comply with the regulations of the British Board of Trade, and our cattle are not allowed to land unless those regulations are observed.

The health of the
animals is infinitely more important than the surroundings in which they are shipped. It was simply because of an alleged outbreak of disease among some of the cattle shipped from this country twenty-five or thirty years ago that our Canadian animals were kept out of the Old Country for so long a period.
The animals are inspected by the officers of the Department of Agriculture. .
It is important to know definitely whether the animals are given adequate accommodation. To whom do the officials report in this regard? Does the inspector report to the minister?

This officer reports to the
Department of Marine and Fisheries if the fittings, and so forth, are in accordance with the regulations.
He measures the space?
Yes.

Who is the inspector at
St. John, and what is the salary?

The inspector, Mr. J. M.
Martin, receives a salary of $300, working part time.

Who is the inspector at
Halifax?

There is no inspector
there.

If we succeed in re-establishing the industry in Nova Scotia, will the minister give us an assurance that 9 p.m. he will appoint an inspector at Halifax and that the department will lend every assistance in building up the trade again?
Most certainly.

Item agreed to.
To continue subsidies for wrecking plants-Quebec and British Columbia, $35,000.

This subsidy applies to
the St. Lawrence and to the west coast. There are two plants in the Maritime provinces, the St. John Shipbuilding Company in New Brunswick, and Beasley Brothers in Halifax. Why does the item discriminate

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
against these firms? Why is this all allotted to one firm on the Pacific coast and one on the Atlantic, without any allotment to the salvage companies of Halifax and St. John?
I would like to ask, Mr. Chairman-
I would like to have an answer, with all due respect to the hon. member for North Winnipeg.

I am informed that in years past we gave a subsidy to a salvage company on the Atlantic coast, but it has been discontinued on account of representations made by other companies interested in salvage work. They preferred to have the competition open to all companies, instead of giving a preference to any one firm. That is the reason.

I quite understand that
they wished to get the work on a purely salvage basis; they make or break, as the case may be. If they win they win big; if they lose, they do not get anything. It seems to me that if there is enough work that scheme should be followed out by the government and the vote should be abolished. I suggest to the minister that he consider the advisability of cuting his vote out here and now. It will save the country $35,000. It has been demonstrated by the minister himself- and I am sure that he was backed up by his deputy, from whom no doubt he got the information-that so far as the Atlantic coast is concerned they do not want a subsidy; they prefer to have it in a go-as-you-please way, taking a chance on the work. There is a well-equipped plant in the city of St. JohD and another, I believe, in Halifax; they are private firms and do work at a profit. They take their chance on getting the work, and on being paid if they are successful. Usually they take work on this basis: if they do not complete the job they get no money at all. It seems to me this principle could well be applied on the St. Lawrence, and there is no necessity for this subsidy to the Davie Shipbuilding Company at Quebec. I invite the minister to delete this item from his estimates this year and thus save the country $35,000.
I would like to ask the minister if these subsidies were granted by tender or by competition, or how they were granted.

The reason for giving this subsidy to the Quebec plant is that first of all it is the only plant on the St. Lawrence river. This plant was not prosperous; it was 14011-146
about to close on account of poor business, and it was represented to the department by the shipping interests that we should give it assistance in order to keep it in operation. The Canadian Pacific Railway has taken over the plant and apparatus and formed a subsidiary company, so in reality they are operating this salvage plant on the St. Lawrence in order to have at least one such plant on that river. It was thought that this establishment, which is very useful to the steamship companies on the St. Lawrence, was about to be closed; the plant is absolutely necessary, and we extended the subsidy, as I desire to insist, upon recommendations made to the department by the shipping interests.

I think the minister has given an additional first class reason why this-vote should be eliminated. In other words the government are giving a subsidy to a great company like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which operates an immense line of shipping on the St. Lawrence and to whom $35,000, or-how much is allotted to the St. Lawrence?
Twenty-five thousand dollars.

That is a mere bagatelle to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If that plant is necessary to the company they will take its cost out of the travelling public, and that amount should be saved to the public. A subsidy is not necessary on the Pacific coast, and I suggest that if a great casualty should happen some ship the salvage facilities of St. John and Halifax could very well be brought up to where they were needed. I again invite the minister to cut out this vote. It is there because it has been there for a good many years. It is like a great many other votes; once they get in the estimates-and I think the minister will be the first to recognize this truism-it takes a team of oxen to get them out again. A great corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway can get along without this subsidy.

This subsidy is not granted merely to meet the requests of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; this plant is absolutely necessary to all navigation companies having boats plying the St. Lawrence. The situation there might be different from that which prevails in the Maritime provinces. There is probably not sufficient work to develop the St. Lawrence plant and have it maintained by a private company. If we do not give a subsidy to this company which now exists, this plant may be done away

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

with and we would be placed in a very embarrassing position. I would not care to take upon myself the responsibility of stopping its operations and thus exposing the government to the very severe and well founded criticism of all the companies drawing benefits from this plant. Navigation on the St. Lawrence is a very important matter, as is navigation everywhere, and the government should take and is trying to take every precaution and every C9re in order to protect navigation. We have been informed that if we do not pay this subsidy the plant'wilil be closed, and what then will be the position of the government? We will be exposed to the criticism of the companies and probably to the criticism of the members, voicing the public interest of this country. I would not care to take the responsibility of dropping this vote, 'because I am convinced that it is absolutely necessary.
If it is necessary at Quebec why is it not necessary at Halifax?

Because there are several
other companies at Halifax, and they have informed the department that they want to be free in competition; they do not want any company subsidized by the government. There is no such thing at Quebec; there is no such thing on the St. Lawrence at all, because there is only one company, which, unassisted, is not capable of making both ends meet.

What about the $10,000
which is given to British Columbia? You have a number of private companies there; why should this company at Quebec be favoured above other companies?

Probably the representations which have been made in regard to British Columbia were similar to those made regarding the St. Lawrence. The situation might be very different from that of the Atlantic coast.

I would like to
point out, Mr. Chairman

I think the minister would
take a great responsibility in eliminating this particular vote with regard to British Columbia and the Pacific coast,

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And Quebec also.

I am not so familiar with Quebec, but I want to say that the salvage companies, keep excellent boats on hand, fully equipped for service. One company recently paid a high price in England for a very power-	I ,	,	: , ,	.
ful tug, one of the most powerful on the Pacific coast, for the purposes of salvage. These boats are kept under steam, and their crews are maintained on their regular wages, ready at all times to proceed to sea on the shortest possible notice, with the result that when a wreck takes place they are able to render immediate assistance and save very often a large amount of money, in many cases perhaps many lives. They are rendering a very excellent service. If this subsidy were wiped out and this work were split up it would probably not be nearly as efficient as it is at present, and the minister would be assuming a very grave risk if he did anything of the kind without first making a very thorough investigation of the situation. The more he investigates it the greater reason I am sure he will find for maintaining this subsidy.

By this subsidy
the government is creating unfair competition with the Atlantic coast. Wreckage occurs, and tenders are asked for salvage of that wreckage. The Atlantic coast companies are handicapped to the extent of the $25,000 which is given to Quebec, to the salvage association there. So far as the Atlantic coast is concerned, we do not want any subsidy for that kind of work, and we do not think-I do not think- that any subsidy should be paid to any company for work of that nature. It is unnecessary. The wrecks are numerous enough, and the work in connection with the salvage of these wrecks is profitable enough, to permit these companies to work without any government assistance at all. I quite agree with my hon. friend from York-Sunbury that there is no occasion for a vote of this kind, and I endorse his suggestion that the minister drop the item from the estimates. It is money that can be well saved. I repeat that the expenditure is unnecessary; it creates unfair competition, and the wrecking companies are doing quite well enough without any government assistance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend
does not suggest that the Atlantic coast companies would come up into the St. Lawrence river to do salvage work there; they would arrive much too long after the accident happened to be of any use. This salvage plant is just as necessary for the equipment of the St. Lawrence route as are the lights and buoys and other aids to navigation which are provided. The salvage plant which was operated by the Davie Company-I happen to know something about it-was operated at a lops.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
It could not continue, and the shipping companies got together and came to the government, and finally the Canadian Pacific railway agreed to take over the plant and operate it with any losses that might occur in operation, provided that the Department of Marine and Fisheries, acting in the interests of the navigation of the St. Lawrence route, as well as for the benefit of all the shipping companies, would pay the subsidy. This salvage plant is needed for the St. Lawrence route, and I am surprised to hear my friend from Halifax suggest that it comes in competition with the Atlantic coast companies. I thought we were friends. I thought Halifax and St. John were interested in the navigation of the St. Lawrence river, using Quebec in the summer and Halifax and St. John in the winter, and I am surprised to see him working against the St. Lawrence route.

My friend from Quebec
East is apparently very anxious that Quebeo should get the whole vote. Neither St. John nor Halifax gets any of it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They do not need it.

Why do they need it in
Quebec?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because the company
was operating at a loss, and it could not go on.

Was it not
efficient?

There is no reason why
the company should not be efficient and make money at Quebec the same as at any other place.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It could not be done.
There is less business than on the Atlantic coast.

The Canadian Pacific will
not go broke on that work. You are just wasting $35,000.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was Minister of Marine and Fisheries when this government came into power in 1921, and this condition existed then. This subsidy was paid by the government, I was going to say of which the hon. member for South Winnipeg was a supporter, but at all events it was paid by the government which most hon. gentlemen immediately opposite w7ere supporting at that time. It was done because it was necessary, and we have to continue this arrangement because it is necessary.

Two wrongs do not make
a right.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is two rights.

In reference to what itjhe Minister of Justice has just said, I wish to call his attention to the Estimates for 1920-21, in which this vote for $35,000 appears, and this is how it read1:
To continue subsidies for wrecking plants in Quebec, Maritime provinces and British Columbia.
So since that time the vote has been changed1.

I feel inclined to agree with those who are opposed to this subsidy. I have heard no good reason given yet why it should be continued. If every concern in Canada that is losing money can come to this government and get a subsidy, there will be no end of applications for subsidies. What I really wish to ask the minister in charge of the department is this: What is the actual amount of work that was done in the St. Lawrence by the company that has received this subsidy for the last few years? What service have they performed for the subsidy of $25,000?

It might be of interest to the committee to know what are the earnings and the expenses of this wrecking plant. Their expenses are $81,000, and their earnings, including the subsidy, are only $56,000. They are receiving from their private work only $31,555.79. They have a loss every year, and the loss last year was $25,136.95.

Surely the minister is not so guileless as not to know how easy it is to show a bookkeeping deficit to suit the circumstances and get a subsidy. It would not be the first time that has been done, and he would not be the first minister. While I am on my feet, let me say that the Minister of Justice cannot get away with any such story as he has told us to-night. Everybody knows that there are more wrecks in the St. Lawrence than on the Atlantic coast around St. John and Halifax, and if the salvage operators at St. John and Halifax are willing to take their chances on this class of work without a subsidy, surely there is some concern on the St. Lawrence that can take the same chance. The way this works out is just this:	The shipping companies
which have losses on the St. Lawrence are probably getting their work done at a very great deal less than the tramp steamers and liners which have to have work of this kind done on the Atlantic coast, because they have to pay on a true salvage basis, and if the salvage operators make a successful job of it they get a large sum in compensation. That is 'how they make money if they make any money a.t alll. There is no longer any real
Supply-Marine and Fisheries

justification for this vote, especially in the light of the circumstances and the information that the minister has given to the committee since this item came before it.

The Minister of
Justice seems to have come to the relief of his colleague in a very heated1 manner; he seems to have lost some of his patience. I want to say to him that I am not attacking the St. Lawrence route. If this subsidy is withdrawn, and if the company which is enoying the subsidy ceases to do the work, I am perfectly satisfied that the combined steamship companies operating on the Atlantic, together with the underwriters, will very soon provide themselves with an efficient salvage plant to take care of any wrecks that may occur. Probably under those conditions they would confine themselves to the St. Lawrence and not get beyond its mouth. I repeat the subsidy is unwarranted, and 1 would again suggest to the minister that it be withdrawn.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at the callous indifference with which hon. gentlemen from the Maritime provinces, after advancing what they think to be good reasons why the Atlantic vote should be reduced or withdrawn, cheerfully propose to throw British Columbia into the discard by simply sweeping away the whole vote without advancing one particle of reason why that province should be discriminated against. I must support the attitude taken by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Tolmie). The company that got this subsidy are, I believe, very good friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, and I have no doubt they support the exMinister of Agriculture, But that is by the way. Their services are absolutely needed on the Pacific coast. We have not got any other private companies there interested in the wrecking business that amount to very much. I think my hon. friend from Victoria will confirm my statement that this wrecking company brought their latest boat out from England last year at enormous expense, it being fitted not only for wrecking purposes but for life-saving, and the subsidy covers the dual services. As my hon. friend said, the steamer is kept at Esquimalt harbour with steam up all the time. What the conditions may be in the east, I do not propose to discuss, but I do not think hon. gentlemen from the Maritimes should try to interfere in regard to this matter with which they are not acquainted. Conditions in British Columbia are totally different to those in the east. Not only that, but if

there is to be any change I would say that the subsidy for British Colombia should be increased. It is well known that the government have gone to some expense, and I give them credit for it, in improving the life-saving appliances on the west coast. It is essential during four months of the year to have a boat of the same character stationed at a .place called Bamfield, where it would be more readily accessible to respond to calls from ships in distress on the west coast than. at Esquimalt, which is too far away. I have always tried to get this boat stationed at Bamfield for the winter months, but they say the subsidy is not sufficient, as they would have to keep another boat at Victoria, and the extra expense would not be justified. For the last three or four years the government has put one of its naval boats, the Thiepval, and one of their trawlers, the Givenchy, on this service. Those boats are very well in their way and are betteT than nothing, but they are quite unsuited, for they have neither the requisite speed nor power. If a boat is disabled on the west coast you need a craft powerful enough, such as that subsidized by the government, to go and pull her offshore before it is too late. The naval boats utilized by the government are not fit for this work for, as I say, they have not sufficient weight and power. But they are better than nothing and have rendered very good service, as the committee will appreciate from a letter whidh I am about to quote:
The Thiepval did very good service during the winter, Lieut. Godfrey in command. Recently he got out of here and got a line aboard the Mexican sailing ship disabled off Garmanah, beating the fast U.S. Snohomish by a few lengths, although she had only a 24-mile run from Flattery.	[DOT]
He concludes his letter in this way:
We are glad that sensible people are running these affairs of the navy and would like them to know of our appreciation.
Nevertheless those boats are not suited for the work. Some time or other they will be called upon to go out and save a lot of passengers or a valuable cargo, but they will be unalble to do so for lack of power. I call on my hon. friend from Victoria to support me that if any change is made in this vote it ought to be by way of increased subsidy to enable that wrecker to be placed on the west coast during the winter months.

Will the minister tell us how many wrecks have occurred along the Atlantic coast, in the St. Lawrence river, and on the Pacific coast?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

I have no record at hand
of wrecks on the Atlantic coast because these estimates do not deal with that part of the work. I had a record of wrecks on the St. Lawrence route where the Quebec Salvage Company is operating. Last year from June to December they rendered assistance to sixteen ships in distress.
Was that for the navigation season of 1925?
Yes.
Has the minister any records of wrecks on the Pacific coast for the same period?

There were fifteen on the
Pacific coast.
Were they all assisted by this salvage company?
Yes.

As practically every member from the eastern provinces is opposed to the part of this subsidy relating to the Atlantic, representing $10,000, and as the minister himself has expressed hi3 agreement with them, I am at a loss to know why he does not reduce the item by that amount.

The subsidy for the
Atlantic ports was dropped three or four years ago. The work is now done under contract.
I understood the minister to say that he was paying $10,000 of this subsidy towards the Atlantic service.

No; $10,000 is for the
Pacific coast.
Of course if it is under contract we have simply got to pay it until the contract expires. How long does the contract run?

The contract with the
Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company was renewed May 1, 1922.
For how long?
Five years.
You have to pay it anyway for five years.

Can the minister give us any
further information in regard to this contract?

It was renewed last year.
It was for a period of ten years from the 2nd of July, 1925.
If the committe had that information a little while ago the discussion would have terminated, because we could not get out of it if we wanted to.
In previous years, I know in 1919 and 1920-a subsidy was given to salvage companies operating on the Atlantic coast. Why was that cut out? Was it at their own request?

It is important to note
that on the Atlantic coast several companies are doing the same work. They are not in the same position as we are on the St. Lawrence route. We have only one company there. There are several companies on the Atlantic coast and they have made representations to the department that they preferred to be free to compete for the work to be done on the Atlantic coast, and we have stopped giving subsidies to the Atlantic companies.
When was that done?
About 1922.

Was that done absolutely on
the request of the wrecking companies?
Yes, on account of the representations made by the companies that no assistance be given to any company; that they preferred to be free to compete for the work.

In other words, one company which has a monopoly of the traffic on the St. Lawrence is not able to make both ends meet, while several companies in St. John, Halifax, Sydney and elsewhere are competing against each other and desire to wipe out all government assistance and1 go ahead on their own account. But they cannot do that in the city of Quebec. I always understood that Quebec was a pap-fed province, and now I know it.

speechtext: Those words will be taken down.

Will the minister
give us an explanation why a bonus should be given to companies from Montreal down the St. Lawrence when it is not given to companies from Montreal up? There is the Donnelly wrecking company of Kingston; they get no assistance. They do all the work in the upper part of the river.

No representation along
those lines has ever been made for assistance to any other port, anywbwe.
Supply-Marine and Fisheries
Does the hon. member not think it a peculiar thing that this company above Montreal can carry on, make money and maintain a big plant, while the companies below Montreal must get assistance?

The figures speak for themselves. This company has expenses of $81,000, and its return, without including the subsidy, is only $31,000. Even with the subsidy of $25,000 that we are giving them, they are making a loss every year of $25,000. Is there any chance of their keeping their plant in operation if we do away with the subsidy? They would certainly close, and the minister of Marine and Fisheries, whoever he .might be-it might be my hon. friend opposite- would be criticized if anything happened.
It is peculiar that one company from Montreal must get a grant, while above Montreal no company asks for a grant.
Possibly the reason is that there is no necessity for assistance.

I think the
minister stated that they gave $10,000 for fifteen wrecks on the Pacific coast.
That was not all for wrecks. Assistance was given to them.

On the St.
Lawrence there were sixteen cases, and the minister states that $25,000 was given for salvaging those cases, why is there such a difference in the figures?

It is comparable to the
case of a man who insures his house. We have to insure and protect the navigation company, and we have to be prepared to proceed to the wrecks and give assistance. We do not know what will happen. A man may pay a premium for many years and his house will never bum, but he is fully justified in paying that premium. We do not know what position we may be placed in, but we are taking the precautions indicated to us as necessary by those who are supposed to know. We are doing this in the same manner as we are giving all the other assistance to navigation in this country. The Minister of Justice has referred to lighthouses, buoys, and so on; we are doing all this to help navigation and to have our waters as safe as possible, to protect the trade of the country. If we should stop such aid now we would have to bear the responsibility.

I suppose you have more
wrecks on the St. Lawrence than you have on the coast?
Judging from the earnings there seem to be less, because they have not enough to meet their obligations.
That would not follow.

On the Atlantic they do
not want the subsidy, and say "Let us compete."
What would be the earnings of the wrecking plant in British Columbia?

I have not a statement
of the earnings and expenses of the British Columbia company.

The minister has frequently stated that owing to the competition among the wrecking firms in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick there is no need for a subsidy being given to any of them. It seems to me that the granting of this subsidy' of $25,000 to one concern on the St. Lawrence tends to prevent competition, because it is only natural that a wrecking company which anticipated going into that business would not think of establishing a plant where there was already a plant subsidized to the extent of $25,000. I suggest that the minister withdraw this subsidy, to encourage competition and obtain the results which we are enjoying in the Maritime provinces. He stated a few moments ago that the St. Lawrence was too far away from the wrecking plants in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I might draw his attention to the fact that we have had successful operation of wrecking plants from Halifax as far east as the straits of Belle Isle, and only two years ago the Beasley firm, well known to members on the other side of the House, successfully salvaged a number of guns from the H.M.S. Renown. If they can do that I submit they can go as far as the St. Lawrence river. The government might well withdraw this subsidy of $25,000-I say nothing about the British Columbia subsidy-and let the companies proceed as they do in the Maritime provinces.

Has the
minister had any request from wrecking companies on the Great Lakes? The minister has some idea of the enormous traffic on those lakes. He has already had a vote passed for the removal of one wreck in the river St. Clair. During the busy season of the year a boat passes that place every seven minutes going down or up the river. I cannot

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
understand why these subsidies should be granted to wrecking companies in the lower part of the St. Lawrence and other parts of Canada and not extended to the Great Lakes if the scheme is considered a feasible one.
No request has been made to the department to subsidize any companies in the territory mentioned by my hon. friend.

This is the fifth session
of parliament that I have brought up this question in connection with this $35,000 item, and I wish to protest on behalf of the ports on the Great Lakes regarding all' these maritime votes not covering the Great Lakes as well as the ocean and river. I want to find out from the minister whether this lis just a vote for the ocean. Where do the Great Lakes come in on this particular proposition? Are the people of the Great Lakes just to be hewers of wood and drawers of water to the ocean and its traffic and to pay the cost thereof? Is this department going to continue to be a political department?-because it has never been anything but a political department for both parties since confederation. It assists certain sections at the expense of the rest of the country. We have passed four or five items to-night but I was not here when two or three of them were being discussed.
The other day I introduced to the minister a delegation representative of all the shipping interests, captains and Canadian lake navigators on the Great Lakes, and he received them very courteously. They were asking for certain reforms in regard to this particular department. The people of the Great Lakes are getting sick and tired of paying taxes and getting nothing at all in return. As I pointed out two or three years ago, these votes should be cancelled altogether at the end of the five year contract period.
This particular item of $35,000 for wrecking plants in Quebec and British Columbia, is mixed up in politics and it should never have been granted by parliament. If you have a vote like this for one or two plants in Quebec and British Columbia, why not have grants for wrecking plants throughout the whole of Canada? Why is there not equality of treatment? The Railway Act provides for equality of treatment in regard to transportation and wrecking plants on land; why is there not .equality of treatment on water? Are we to continue as in the days of John and Sebastian Cabot and Christopher Columbus, who never heard of the Great Lakes? The department has always been a political department and will always continue to be as long as the
ports on the Great Lakes fall for it. I am sorry to say that when this vote has been up in this House during the last three or four sessions the members from Ontario have been afraid to get up in their places and speak about it.
In front of the Niagara there is a large sand shoal where there a wreck may occur to any of the wonderful boats which carry a million and a half passengers a year, yet the government will do nothing. We have pointed this out to the government. I do not blame the present government at all in regard to this matter because the late government was just as bad. The quicker the Department of Marine and Fisheries gets out of politics the better.
I received a letter from Commodore George
H.	Gooderham, of the Royal Canadian Yacht Club, Toronto, asking that certain shoals in the bay of Quinte and the Murray and Trent canals be removed, but four or five years passed and nothing was done. They had a wreck in Toronto off the exhibition on the Modgeska and a very fine officer, Captain Henderson, lost his certificate. Why? Because the wreck commissioner was an oceangoing officer who did not understand lake waters, and he cut off the certificate of a man who knew more than the wreck commissioner did. I am pointing this out just because you, Mr. Chairman, have been a good friend of the Great Lakes. The day is coming when the general policy of the government regarding Dominion services such as aids to navigation, wrecking plants, life-saving, navigation schools, examinations of masters and mates and all these other items we have passed to-night, should extend not only to the St. [DOT]Lawrence and the gulf but right to the head of the lakes.
On lake Superior and lake Huron wrecks occur in bad weather, and if you look around for a wrecking plant you cannot get one. On lake Ontario conditions are so bad that you have to get a private wrecking plant at Kingston, and it may have to go two or three hundred miles to reach the scene of the accident. A Dominion government dredge, the Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was wrecked off Newcastle in a storm involving a cost of $700,000, and it took seven years to find it. They had to import wrecking plants from Germany and other parts of the world to find where that dredge was, and they discovered it in about sixty feet of water off Newcastle.
I do not oppose this vote at all. It may be necessary. I pointed out, as reported in Hansard of 1922, 1923, 1924 and 1925, that if you are to apply a general policy of subsidizing

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
private wrecking plants in Quebec and British Columbia, and other aid from this department, that general policy should apply to the Great Lakes as well as the ocean and the gulf. If 'you read the returns of the Department of Marine and Fisheries you will realize what a great tonnage there is on the Great Lakes without any wrecking plant or aids to navigation, and yet sectional interests are allowed to interfere with the work of this department. There is a good deputy at the head of this department. The present minister, whom I met with a delegation of people on both sides of politics, received us courteously, and we were pleased with the reception we got. This policy should be extended to the Great Lakes, in view of the memorandum which has been laid before the government by the shipping interests on the Great Lakes and by the captains and mates who have to sail boats on those waters in season and out of season, in all kinds of weather, and who have to put up with the intolerable state of affairs on the lakes, such as lack of aids to navigation, lack of proper lighthouses, lack of proper wrecking plants and proper lifesaving equipment.
We in the city of Toronto have to be a sort of Department of Marine and Fisheries for lake Ontario, the Niagara river, lake Erie, the Muskoka lakes and Georgian bay when our citizens go there in the summer time. If the government are to vote $2,500,000 along these lines there should be reciprocal treatment between the ports on the ocean and ports on the Great Lakes. I would support liberal expenditure for ocean shipping. We hear talk about Maritime rights and British Columbia rights, and nothing should be too good for these distant provinces; but when the port of Toronto, which contributes large sums to the Dominion treasury, has to spend its own money on aids to navigation, the Marine and Fisheries department should see that traffic on the Great Lakes gets a fair share of this vote. We ought to know what these wrecking plants do, what they cost, what dividends they pay, what insurance they have-in a word, what justification there is for this expenditure. I should think that in the course of five years the government would have been able to devise a policy of its own in this matter. I certainly must protest against the discrimination against the Great Lakes while maritime ports are being taken care of. The lake ports are becoming an important factor in transportation to-day and when we consider what the United States gov-
{Mr. Church.]
emment is doing at Cleveland, Buffalo, Toledo, Detroit and elsewhere, we are astounded at the way in which navigation on the lakes on this side is being neglected. The United States government is doing everything it possibly can to aid navigation, in the provision of buoys, beacon lights, lighthouses and all other necessary equipment. It is small wonder that there has taken place in this country one of the biggest mergers we have ever seen.
I appeal to the minister to make a thorough survey of the situation on the Great Lakes. The matter was brought clearly to his attention in an elaborate memorandum submitted to him by the delegation which I had the honour to introduce, comprising representatives from various lake ports, who asked that the vote be extended to include provision for aid to navigation on the Great Lakes. I trust that the matter will receive the serious attention of the government.
What do the contracts call for ?

Under the contract with the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company the steamer Lord Strathcona must be maintained in service, together with such plant as may be required, to the satisfaction of the department. The service extends from May 1 to December 1.

Just what has the
steamer to do?
It is required to assist vessels in distress in any accident that occurs in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Upon what basis is the subsidy granted? Does it depend upon the value of the plant or the number of wrecks?

The amount is arbitrary,
and if the company is able to show a surplus it is supposed to divide it with the department.

I notice that in one case the
grant is $25,000 and in the other $10,000. Is the smaller amount given to British Columbia because they could get along with $10,000, while owing to disasters Quebec found it necessary to ask for $25,000?

Unfortunately I cannot
give the details of the transaction. I was not in the department when it was entered into.

I do not suppose the British
Columbia company would Tefuse $25,000?

Minister of Labour

I am sure not, but they
were satisfied with $10,000.

Perhaips that was all they
could get. But viewing the matter from a business standpoint there is pal-
10 pun. pably some reason for giving one concern $25,000 and the other $10,000. Possibly the distribution is based upon the number of wrecks, the amount of capital involved, or some other consideration. The minister has not explained this point.

In British Columbia the
company is free to operate the whole year round, and in that way is in a position to earn money in addition to the grant. In Quebec, on the other hand, they operate only during part of the year. This explains it in part. The investment is the same in both cases, but there is the difference in duration of earning capacity.

What amount did British
Columbia require-just the $10,000?
Ten thousand was satisfactory to them. They requested a renewal of the contract.

Is it the same as the contract
of last year?
The contract has been the same for ten years.

Has any other salvage
company in Quebec applied to the government for a similar subsidy?
No, this is the only one.

How
many wrecks have been removed on the lower St. Lawrence during the past two years?

This vote is not exactly
to provide for the removal of wrecks; it is for assistance to be given to ships in distress.

Has the
minister a statement of such aid given?
We have a statement, yes, although I have not given it in detail. The company has been called upon to render assistance in sixteen instances.
